entries.5f25bfb1164fca250d824ca546dccb3f7a28026d: <div sID="gen9991" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="31" osisID="Job.31" sID="Job.31"/> <div eID="gen9991" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9992" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen9993" type="x-p"/> Job had often protested his integrity in general; here he does it in particular instances, not in a way of commendation (for he does not here proclaim his good deeds), but in his own just and necessary vindication, to clear himself from those crimes with which his friends had falsely charged him, which is a debt every man owes to his own reputation. Job's friends had been particular in their articles of impeachment against him, and therefore he is so in his protestation, which seems to refer especially to what Eliphaz had accused him of, <reference osisRef="Job.22.6-Job.22.9">ch. xxii. 6</reference>, &c. They had produced no witnesses against him, neither could they prove the things whereof they now accused him, and therefore he may well be admitted to purge himself upon oath, which he does very solemnly, and with many awful imprecations of God's wrath if he were guilty of those crimes. This protestation confirms God's character of him, that there was none like him in the earth. Perhaps some of his accusers durst not have joined with him; for he not only acquits himself from those gross sins which lie open to the eye of the world, but from many secret sins which, if he had been guilty of them, nobody could have charged him, with, because he will prove himself no hypocrite. Nor does he only maintain the cleanness of his practices, but shows also that in them he went upon good principles, that the reason of his eschewing evil was because he feared God, and his piety was at the bottom of his justice and charity; and this crowns the proof of his sincerity. I. The sins from which he here acquits himself are, 1. Wantonness and uncleanness of heart, <reference osisRef="Job.31.1-Job.31.4">ver. 1-4</reference>. 2. Fraud and injustice in commerce, <reference osisRef="Job.31.4-Job.31.8">ver. 4-8</reference>. 3. Adultery, <reference osisRef="Job.31.9-Job.31.12">ver. 9-12</reference>. 4. Haughtiness and severity towards his servants, <reference osisRef="Job.31.13-Job.31.15">ver. 13-15</reference>. 5. Unmercifulness to the poor, the widows, and the fatherless, <reference osisRef="Job.31.16-Job.31.23">ver. 16-23</reference>. 6. Confidence in his worldly wealth, <reference osisRef="Job.31.24-Job.31.25">ver. 24, 25</reference>. 7. Idolatry, <reference osisRef="Job.31.26-Job.31.28">ver. 26-28</reference>. 8. Revenge, <reference osisRef="Job.31.29-Job.31.31">ver. 29-31</reference>. 9. Neglect of poor strangers, <reference osisRef="Job.31.32">ver. 32</reference>. 10. Hypocrisy in concealing his own sins and cowardice in conniving at the sins of others, <reference osisRef="Job.31.33-Job.31.34">ver. 33, 34</reference>. 11. Oppression, and the violent invasion of other people's rights, <reference osisRef="Job.31.38-Job.31.40">ver. 38-40</reference>. And towards the close, he appeals to God's judgment concerning his integrity, <reference osisRef="Job.31.35-Job.31.37">ver. 35-37</reference>. Now, II. In all this we may see, 1. The sense of the patriarchal age concerning good and evil and what was so long ago condemned as sinful, that is, both hateful and hurtful. 2. A noble pattern of piety and virtue proposed to us for our imitation, which, if our consciences can witness for us that we conform to it, will be our rejoicing, as it was Job's in the day of evil.
entries.b31a864a5f124adce345ebe28aa78e1ab4d6c800: <div eID="gen9993" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen9992" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Job's Vindication of Himself. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1520.)</title> <div sID="gen9994" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> I made a covenant with mine eyes; why then should I think upon a maid? <hi type="super">2</hi> For what portion of God <hi type="italic">is there</hi> from above? and <hi type="italic">what</hi> inheritance of the Almighty from on high? <hi type="super">3</hi> <hi type="italic">Is</hi> not destruction to the wicked? and a strange <hi type="italic">punishment</hi> to the workers of iniquity? <hi type="super">4</hi> Doth not he see my ways, and count all my steps? <hi type="super">5</hi> If I have walked with vanity, or if my foot hath hasted to deceit; <hi type="super">6</hi> Let me be weighed in an even balance, that God may know mine integrity. <hi type="super">7</hi> If my step hath turned out of the way, and mine heart walked after mine eyes, and if any blot hath cleaved to mine hands; <hi type="super">8</hi> <hi type="italic">Then</hi> let me sow, and let another eat; yea, let my offspring be rooted out. <div eID="gen9994" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9995" type="x-p"/> The lusts of the flesh, and the love of the world, are the two fatal rocks on which multitudes split; against these Job protests he was always careful to stand upon his guard. <div eID="gen9995" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9996" type="x-p"/> I. Against the lusts of the flesh. He not only kept himself clear from adultery, from defiling his neighbour's wives (<reference osisRef="Job.31.9">v. 9</reference>), but from all lewdness with any women whatsoever. He kept no concubine, no mistress, but was inviolably faithful to the marriage bed, though his wife was none of the wisest, best, or kindest. From the beginning it was so, that a man should have but one wife and cleave to her only; and Job kept closely to that institution and abhorred the thought of transgressing it; for, though his greatness might tempt him to it, his goodness kept him from it. Job was now in pain and sickness of body, and under that affliction it is in a particular manner comfortable if our consciences can witness for us that we have been careful to preserve our bodies in chastity and to possess those vessels in sanctification and honour, pure from the lusts of uncleanness. Now observe here, <div eID="gen9996" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9997" type="x-p"/> 1. What the resolutions were which, in this matter, he kept to (<reference osisRef="Job.31.1">v. 1</reference>): <hi type="italic">I made a covenant with my eyes,</hi> that is, "I watched against the occasions of the sin; <hi type="italic">why then should I think upon a maid?</hi>" that is, "by that means, through the grace of God, I kept myself from the very first step towards it." So far was he from wanton dalliances, or any act of lasciviousness, that, (1.) He would not so much as admit a wanton look. <hi type="italic">He made a covenant with his eyes,</hi> made this bargain with them, that he would allow them the pleasure of beholding the light of the sun and the glory of God shining in the visible creation, provided they would never fasten upon any object that might occasion any impure imaginations, much less any impure desires, in his mind; and under this penalty, that, if they did, they must smart for it in penitential tears. Note, Those that would keep their hearts pure must guard their eyes, which are both the outlets and inlets of uncleanness. Hence we read of <hi type="italic">wanton</hi> eyes (<reference osisRef="Isa.3.16">Isa. iii. 16</reference>) and <hi type="italic">eyes full of adultery,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.14">2 Pet. ii. 14</reference>. The first sin began in the eye, <reference osisRef="Gen.3.6">Gen. iii. 6</reference>. What we must not meddle with we must not lust after; and what we must not lust after we must not look at; not the forbidden wealth (<reference osisRef="Prov.23.5">Prov. xxiii. 5</reference>), not the forbidden wine (<reference osisRef="Prov.23.31">Prov. xxiii. 31</reference>), not the forbidden woman, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.28">Matt. v. 28</reference>. (2.) He would not so much as allow a wanton thought: "<hi type="italic">Why then should I think upon a maid</hi> with any unchaste fancy or desire towards her?" Shame and sense of honour might restrain him from soliciting the chastity of a beautiful virgin, but only grace and the fear of God would restrain him from so much as thinking of it. Those are not chaste that are not so in spirit as well as body, <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.34">1 Cor. vii. 34</reference>. See how Christ's exposition of the seventh commandment agrees with the ancient sense of it, and how much better Job understood it than the Pharisees, though they sat in Moses's chair. <div eID="gen9997" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9998" type="x-p"/> 2. What the reasons were which, in this matter, he was governed by. It was not for fear of reproach among men, though that is to be considered (<reference osisRef="Prov.6.33">Prov. vi. 33</reference>), but for fear of the wrath and curse of God. He knew very well, (1.) That uncleanness is a sin that forfeits all good, and shuts us out from the hope of it (<reference osisRef="Job.31.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">What portion of God is there from above?</hi> What blessing can such impure sinners expect from the pure and holy God, or what token of his favour? What inheritance of the Almighty can they look for from on high? There is no portion, no inheritance, no true happiness, for a soul, but what is in God, in the Almighty, and what comes from above, from on high. Those that wallow in uncleanness render themselves utterly unfit for communion with God, either in grace here or in glory hereafter, and become allied to unclean spirits, which are for ever separated from him; and then what portion, what inheritance, can they have with God? No unclean thing shall enter into the New Jerusalem, that holy city. (2.) It is a sin that incurs divine vengeance, <reference osisRef="Job.31.3">v. 3</reference>. It will certainly be the sinner's ruin if it be not repented of in time. <hi type="italic">Is not destruction,</hi> a swift and sure destruction, <hi type="italic">to</hi> those <hi type="italic">wicked</hi> people, <hi type="italic">and a strange punishment to the workers of</hi> this <hi type="italic">iniquity?</hi> Fools make a mock at this sin, make a jest of it; it is with them a peccadillo, a trick of youth. But they deceive themselves with vain words, for because of these things, how light soever they make of them, the wrath of God, the unsupportable wrath of the eternal God, <hi type="italic">comes upon the children of disobedience,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.5.6">Eph. v. 6</reference>. There are some sinners whom God sometimes out of the common road of Providence to meet with; such are these. The destruction of Sodom is a strange punishment. <hi type="italic">Is there not alienation</hi> (so some read it) <hi type="italic">to the workers of iniquity?</hi> This is the sinfulness of the sin that it alienates the mind from God (<reference osisRef="Eph.4.18-Eph.4.19">Eph. iv. 18, 19</reference>), and this is the punishment of the sinners that they shall be eternally set at a distance from him, <reference osisRef="Rev.22.15">Rev. xxii. 15</reference>. (3.) It cannot be hidden from the all-seeing God. A wanton thought cannot be so close, nor a wanton look so quick, as to escape his cognizance, much less any act of uncleanness so secretly done as to be out of his sight. If Job was at any time tempted to this sin, he restrained himself from it, and all approaches to it, with this pertinent thought (<reference osisRef="Job.31.4">v. 4</reference>), <hi type="italic">Doth not he see my ways;</hi> as Joseph did (<reference osisRef="Gen.39.9">Gen. xxxix. 9</reference>), <hi type="italic">How can I do it, and sin against God?</hi> Two things Job had an eye to:—[1.] God's omniscience. It is a great truth that God's eyes are <hi type="italic">upon all the ways of men</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.5.20-Prov.5.21">Prov. v. 20, 21</reference>); but Job here mentions it with application to himself and his own actions: <hi type="italic">Doth not he see my ways? O God! thou hast searched me and known me.</hi> God sees what rule we walk by, what company we walk with, what end we walk towards, and therefore what ways we walk in. [2.] His observance. "He not only sees, but takes notice; he <hi type="italic">counts all my steps,</hi> all my false steps in the way of duty, all my by-steps into the way of sin." He not only sees our ways in general, but takes cognizance of our particular steps in these ways, every action, every motion. He keeps account of all, because he will call us to account, will bring every work into judgment. God takes a more exact notice of us than we do of ourselves; for who ever counted his own steps? yet God counts them. Let us therefore walk circumspectly. <div eID="gen9998" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9999" type="x-p"/> II. He stood upon his guard against the love of the world, and carefully avoided all sinful indirect means of getting wealth. He dreaded all forbidden profit as much as all forbidden pleasure. Let us see, <div eID="gen9999" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10000" type="x-p"/> 1. What his protestation is. In general, he had been honest and just in all his dealings, and never, to his knowledge, did any body any wrong. (1.) He never <hi type="italic">walked with vanity</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.31.5">v. 5</reference>), that is, he never durst tell a lie to get a good bargain. It was never his way to banter, or equivocate, or make many words in his dealings. Some men's constant walk is a constant cheat. They either make what they have more than it is, that they may be trusted, or less than it is, that nothing may be expected from them. But Job was a different man. His wealth was not acquired by vanity, though now diminished, <reference osisRef="Prov.13.11">Prov. xiii. 11</reference>. (2.) He never <hi type="italic">hasted to deceit.</hi> Those that deceive must be quick and sharp, but Job's quickness and sharpness were never turned that way. He never made haste to be rich by deceit, but always acted cautiously, lest, through inconsideration, he should do an unjust thing. Note, What we have in the world may be either used with comfort or lost with comfort if it was honestly obtained. (3.) His <hi type="italic">steps never turned out of the way,</hi> the way of justice and fair dealing; from that he never deviated, <reference osisRef="Job.31.7">v. 7</reference>. He not only took care not to walk in a constant course and way of deceit, but he did not so much as take one step out of the way of honesty. In every particular action and affair we must closely tie ourselves up to the rules of righteousness. (4.) His heart did not <hi type="italic">walk after his eyes,</hi> that is, he did not covet what he saw that was another's, nor wish it his own. Covetousness is called the <hi type="italic">lust of the eye,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.2.16">1 John ii. 16</reference>. Achan saw, and then took, the accursed thing. That heart must needs wander that walks after the eyes; for then it looks no further than the things that are seen, whereas it ought to be in heaven whither the eyes cannot reach: it should follow the dictates of religion and right reason: if it follow the eye, it will be misled to that for which <hi type="italic">God will bring men into judgment,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.9">Eccl. xi. 9</reference>. (5.) That <hi type="italic">no blot had cleaved to his hands,</hi> that is, he was not chargeable with getting any thing dishonestly, or keeping that which was another's, whenever it appeared to be so. Injustice is a blot, a blot to the estate, a blot to the owner; it spoils the beauty of both, and therefore is to be dreaded. Those that deal much in the world may perhaps have a blot come upon their hands, but they must wash it off again by repentance and restitution, and not let it <hi type="italic">cleave to their hands.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Isa.33.15">Isa. xxxiii. 15</reference>. <div eID="gen10000" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10001" type="x-p"/> 2. How he ratifies his protestation. So confident is he of his own honesty that, (1.) He is willing to have his goods searched (<reference osisRef="Job.31.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">Let me be weighed in an even balance,</hi> that is, "Let what I have got be enquired into and it will be found to weigh well"—a sign that it was not obtained by vanity, for then <hi type="italic">Tekel</hi> would have been written on it—<hi type="italic">weighed in the balance and found too light.</hi> An honest man is so far from dreading a trial that he desires it rather, being well assured that God knows his integrity and will approve it, and that the trial of it will be to his praise and honour. (2.) He is willing to forfeit the whole cargo if there be found any prohibited or contraband goods, any thing but what he came honestly by (<reference osisRef="Job.31.8">v. 8</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Let me sow, and let another eat,</hi>" which was already agreed to be the doom of oppressors (<reference osisRef="Job.5.5">ch. v. 5</reference>), "and <hi type="italic">let my offspring,</hi> all the trees that I have planted, <hi type="italic">be rooted out.</hi>" This intimates that he believed the sin did deserve this punishment, that usually it is thus punished, but that though now his estate was ruined (and at such a time, if ever, his conscience would have brought his sin to his mind), yet he knew himself innocent and would venture all the poor remains of his estate upon the issue of the trial.
entries.31617bd0717422c13a5a25087ff330a0f40c4295: <div eID="gen10001" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10002" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> If mine heart have been deceived by a woman, or <hi type="italic">if</hi> I have laid wait at my neighbour's door; 10 <hi type="italic">Then</hi> let my wife grind unto another, and let others bow down upon her. <hi type="super">11</hi> For this <hi type="italic">is</hi> a heinous crime; yea, it <hi type="italic">is</hi> an iniquity <hi type="italic">to be punished by</hi> the judges. <hi type="super">12</hi> For it <hi type="italic">is</hi> a fire <hi type="italic">that</hi> consumeth to destruction, and would root out all mine increase. <hi type="super">13</hi> If I did despise the cause of my manservant or of my maidservant, when they contended with me; <hi type="super">14</hi> What then shall I do when God riseth up? and when he visiteth, what shall I answer him? <hi type="super">15</hi> Did not he that made me in the womb make him? and did not one fashion us in the womb? <div eID="gen10002" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10003" type="x-p"/> Two more instances we have here of Job's integrity:— <div eID="gen10003" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10004" type="x-p"/> I. That he had a very great abhorrence of the sin of adultery. As he did not wrong his own marriage bed by keeping a concubine (he did not so much as think upon a maid, <reference osisRef="Job.31.1">v. 1</reference>), so he was careful not to offer any injury to his neighbour's marriage bed. Let us see here, 1. How clear he was from this sin, <reference osisRef="Job.31.9">v. 9</reference>. (1.) He did not so much as covet his neighbour's wife; for even <hi type="italic">his heart was not deceived by a woman.</hi> The beauty of another man's wife did not kindle in him any unchaste desires, nor was he ever moved by the allurements of an adulterous woman, such as is described, <reference osisRef="Prov.7.6-Prov.7.21">Prov. vii. 6</reference>, &c. See the original of all the defilements of the life; they come from a deceived heart. Every sin is deceitful, and none more so than the sin of uncleanness. (2.) He never compassed or imagined any unchaste design. He never <hi type="italic">laid wait at his neighbour's door,</hi> to get an opportunity to debauch his wife in his absence, when the good man was not at home, <reference osisRef="Prov.7.19">Prov. vii. 19</reference>. See <reference osisRef="Job.24.15">ch. xxiv. 15</reference>. 2. What a dread he had of this sin, and what frightful apprehensions he had concerning the malignity of it—that it was a <hi type="italic">heinous crime</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.31.11">v. 11</reference>), one of the greatest vilest sins a man can be guilty of, highly provoking to God, and destructive to the prosperity of the soul. With respect to the mischievousness of it, and the punishment it deserved, he owns that, if he were guilty of that heinous crime, (1.) His family might justly be made infamous in the highest degree (<reference osisRef="Job.31.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">Let my wife grind to another.</hi> Let her be a <hi type="italic">slave</hi> (so some), a <hi type="italic">harlot,</hi> so others. God often punishes the sins of one with the sin of another, the adultery of the husband with the adultery of the wife, as in David's case (<reference osisRef="2Sam.12.11">2 Sam. xii. 11</reference>), which does not in the least excuse the treachery of the adulterous wife; but, how unrighteous soever she is, God is righteous. See <reference osisRef="Hos.4.13">Hos. iv. 13</reference>, <hi type="italic">Your spouses shall commit adultery.</hi> Note, Those who are not just and faithful to their relations must not think it strange if their relations be unjust and unfaithful to them. (2.) He himself might justly be made a public example: <hi type="italic">For it is an iniquity to be punished by the judges;</hi> yea, though those who are guilty of it are themselves judges, as Job was. Note, Adultery is a crime which the civil magistrate ought to take cognizance of and punish: so it was adjudged even in the patriarchal age, before the law of Moses made it capital. It is an evil work, to which the sword of justice ought to be a terror. (3.) It might justly become the ruin of his estate; nay, he knew it would be so (<reference osisRef="Job.31.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">It is a fire.</hi> Lust is a fire in the soul: those that indulge it are said to burn. It consumes all that is good there (the convictions, the comforts), and lays the conscience waste. It kindles the fire of God's wrath, which, if not extinguished by the blood of Christ, will burn to the lowest hell. It will <hi type="italic">consume</hi> even <hi type="italic">to</hi> that eternal <hi type="italic">destruction.</hi> It consumes the body, <reference osisRef="Prov.5.11">Prov. v. 11</reference>. It consumes the substance; it <hi type="italic">roots out all the increase.</hi> Burning lusts bring burning judgments. Perhaps it alludes to the burning of Sodom, which was intended for an example to those who should afterwards, in like manner, live ungodly. <div eID="gen10004" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10005" type="x-p"/> II. That he had a very great tenderness for his servants and ruled them with a gentle hand. He had a great household and he managed it well. By this he evidenced his sincerity that he had grace to govern his passion as well as his appetite; and he that in these two things has the rule of his own spirit is <hi type="italic">better than the mighty,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.16.32">Prov. xvi. 32</reference>. Here observe, 1. What were Job's condescensions to his servants (<reference osisRef="Job.31.13">v. 13</reference>): He did not <hi type="italic">despise the cause of his man-servant,</hi> no, nor of his <hi type="italic">maid-servant, when they contended with him.</hi> If they contradicted him in any thing, he was willing to hear their reasons. If they had offended him, or were accused to him, he would patiently hear what they had to say for themselves, in their own vindication or excuse. Nay, if they complained of any hardship he put upon them, he did not browbeat them, and bid them hold their tongues, but gave them leave to tell their story, and redressed their grievances as far as it appeared they had right on their side. He was tender of them, not only when they served and pleased him, but even when they contended with him. Herein he was a great example to masters, to <hi type="italic">give to their servants that which is just and equal;</hi> nay, to do the same things to them that they expect from them (<reference osisRef="Col.4.1">Col. iv. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.6.9">Eph. vi. 9</reference>), and not to rule them with rigour, and carry it with a high hand. Many of Job's servants were slain in his service (<reference osisRef="Job.1.15-Job.1.17">ch. i. 15-17</reference>); the rest were unkind and undutiful to him, and despised his cause, though he never despised theirs (<reference osisRef="Job.19.15-Job.19.16">ch. xix. 15, 16</reference>); but he had this comfort that in his prosperity he had behaved well towards them. Note, When relations are either removed from us or embittered to us the testimony of our consciences that we have done our duty to them will be a great support and comfort to us. 2. What were the considerations that moved him to treat his servants thus kindly. He had, herein, an eye to God, both as his Judge and their Maker. (1.) As his Judge. He considered, "If I should be imperious and severe with my servants, <hi type="italic">what then shall I do when God riseth up?</hi>" He considered that he had a Master in heaven, to whom he was accountable, who will rise up and will visit; and <hi type="italic">we</hi> are concerned to consider <hi type="italic">what we shall do in the day of his visitation</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.3">Isa. x. 3</reference>), and, considering that we should be undone if God should then be strict and severe with us, we ought to be very mild and gentle towards all with whom we have to do. Consider what would become of us if God should be extreme to mark what we do amiss, should take all advantages against us and insist upon all his just demands from us—if he should visit every offence, and take every forfeiture—if he should always chide, and keep his anger for ever. And let not us be rigorous with our inferiors. Consider what will become of us if we be cruel and unmerciful to our brethren. The cries of the injured will be heard; the sins of the injurious will be punished. Those that showed no mercy shall find none; and what shall we do then? (2.) As his and his servants' Creator, <reference osisRef="Job.31.15">v. 15</reference>. When he was tempted to be harsh with his servants, to deny them their right and turn a deaf ear to their reasonings, this thought came very seasonably into his mind, "<hi type="italic">Did not he that made me in the womb make him?</hi> I am a creature as well as he, and my being is derived and depending as well as his. He partakes of the same nature that I do and is the work of the same hand: <hi type="italic">Have we not all one Father?</hi>" Note, Whatever difference there is among men in their outward condition, in their capacity of mind, or strength of body, or place in the world, he that made the one made the other also, which is a good reason why we should not mock at men's natural infirmities, nor trample upon those that are in any way our inferiors, but, in every thing, do as we would be done by. It is a rule of justice, <hi type="italic">Parium par sit ratio—Let equals be equally estimated and treated;</hi> and therefore since there is so great a parity among men, they being all made of the same mould, by the same power, for the same end, notwithstanding the disparity of our outward condition, we are bound so far to set ourselves upon the level with those we deal with as to do to them, in all respects, as we would they should do to us.
entries.f7e4e1b3a21148741e4e94566cb7d7688ace5172: <div eID="gen10005" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Job's Compassion to the Poor. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1520.)</title> <div sID="gen10006" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> If I have withheld the poor from <hi type="italic">their</hi> desire, or have caused the eyes of the widow to fail; <hi type="super">17</hi> Or have eaten my morsel myself alone, and the fatherless hath not eaten thereof; <hi type="super">18</hi> (For from my youth he was brought up with me, as <hi type="italic">with</hi> a father, and I have guided her from my mother's womb;) <hi type="super">19</hi> If I have seen any perish for want of clothing, or any poor without covering; <hi type="super">20</hi> If his loins have not blessed me, and <hi type="italic">if</hi> he were <hi type="italic">not</hi> warmed with the fleece of my sheep; <hi type="super">21</hi> If I have lifted up my hand against the fatherless, when I saw my help in the gate: <hi type="super">22</hi> <hi type="italic">Then</hi> let mine arm fall from my shoulder blade, and mine arm be broken from the bone. <hi type="super">23</hi> For destruction <hi type="italic">from</hi> God <hi type="italic">was</hi> a terror to me, and by reason of his highness I could not endure. <div eID="gen10006" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10007" type="x-p"/> Eliphaz had particularly charged Job with unmercifulness to the poor (<reference osisRef="Job.22.6-Job.22.9">ch. xxii. 6</reference>, &c.): Thou hast <hi type="italic">withholden bread from the hungry, stripped the naked of their clothing,</hi> and sent <hi type="italic">widows away empty.</hi> One would think he could not have been so very positive and express in his charge unless there had been some truth in it, some ground, for it; and yet it appears, by Job's protestation, that it was utterly false and groundless; he was never guilty of any such thing. See here, <div eID="gen10007" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10008" type="x-p"/> I. The testimony which Job's conscience gave in concerning his constant behaviour towards the poor. He enlarges most upon this head because in this matter he was most particularly accused. He solemnly protests, <div eID="gen10008" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10009" type="x-p"/> 1. That he had never been wanting to do good to them, as there was occasion, to the utmost of his ability. He was always compassionate to the poor, and careful of them, especially the widows and fatherless, that were destitute of help. (1.) He was always ready to grant their desires and answer their expectations, <reference osisRef="Job.31.16">v. 16</reference>. If a poor person begged a kindness of his, he was ready to gratify him; if he could but perceive by the widow's mournful craving look that she expected an alms from him, though she had not confidence enough to ask it, he had compassion enough to give it, and <hi type="italic">never caused the eyes of the widow to fail.</hi> (2.) He put a respect upon the poor, and did them honour; for he took the fatherless children to eat with him at his own table: they should fare as he fared, and be familiar with him, and he would show himself pleased with their company as if they had been his own, <reference osisRef="Job.31.17">v. 17</reference>. As it is one of the greatest grievances of poverty that it exposes to contempt, so it is none of the least supports to the poor to be respected. (3.) He was very tender of them, and had a fatherly concern for them, <reference osisRef="Job.31.18">v. 18</reference>. He was a father to the fatherless, took care of orphans, brought them up with him under his own eye, and gave them, not only maintenance, but education. He was a guide to the widow, who had lost the guide of her youth; he advised her in her affairs, took cognizance of them, and undertook the management of them. Those that need not our alms may yet have occasion for our counsel, and it may be a real kindness to them. This Job says he did <hi type="italic">from his youth, from his mother's womb.</hi> He had something of tenderness and compassion woven in his nature; he began betimes to do good, ever since he could remember; he had always some poor widow or fatherless child under his care. His parents taught him betimes to pity and relieve the poor, and brought up orphans with him. (4.) He provided food convenient for them; they ate of the same morsels that he did (<reference osisRef="Job.31.17">v. 17</reference>), did not eat after him, of the crumbs that fell from his table, but with him, of the best dish upon his table. Those that have abundance must not eat their morsels alone, as if they had none but themselves to take care of, nor indulge their appetite with a dainty bit by themselves, but take others to share with them, as David took Mephibosheth. (5.) He took particular care to clothe those that were without covering, which would be more expensive to him than feeding them, <reference osisRef="Job.31.19">v. 19</reference>. Poor people may perish for want of clothing as well as for want of food—for want of clothing to lie in by night or to go abroad in by day. If Job knew of any that were in this distress, he was forward to relieve them, and instead of giving rich and gaudy liveries to his servants, while the poor were turned off with rags that were ready to be thrown to the dunghill, he had good warm strong clothes made on purpose for them of <hi type="italic">the fleece of his sheep</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.31.20">v. 20</reference>), so that their <hi type="italic">loins,</hi> whenever they girt those garments about them, <hi type="italic">blessed him;</hi> they commended his charity, blessed God for him, and prayed God to bless him. Job's sheep were burned with fire from heaven, but this was his comfort that, when he had them, he came honestly by them, and used them charitably, fed the poor with their flesh and clothed them with their wool. <div eID="gen10009" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10010" type="x-p"/> 2. That he had never been accessory to the wronging of any that were poor. It might be said, perhaps, that he was kind here and there to a poor orphan that was a favourite, but to others he was oppressive. No, he was tender to all and injurious to none. He never so much as <hi type="italic">lifted up his hand against the fatherless</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.31.21">v. 21</reference>), never threatened or frightened them, or offered to strike them; never used his power to crush those that stood in his way or squeeze what he could out of them, though he <hi type="italic">saw his help in the gate,</hi> that is, though he had interest enough, both in the people and in the judges, both to enable him to do it and to bear him out when he had done it. Those that have it in their power to do a wrong thing and go through with it, and a prospect of getting by it, and yet do justly, and love mercy, and are firm to both, may afterwards reflect upon their conduct with much comfort, as Job does here. <div eID="gen10010" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10011" type="x-p"/> II. The imprecation with which he confirms this protestation (<reference osisRef="Job.31.22">v. 22</reference>): "If I have been oppressive to the poor, <hi type="italic">let my arm fall from my shoulder-blade and my arm be broken from the bone,</hi>" that is, "let the flesh rot off from the bone and one bone be disjointed and broken off from another." Had he not been perfectly clear in this matter, he durst not thus have challenged the divine vengeance. And he intimates that it is a righteous thing with God to break the arm that is lifted up against the fatherless, as he withered Jeroboam's arm that was stretched out against a prophet. <div eID="gen10011" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10012" type="x-p"/> III. The principles by which Job was restrained from all uncharitableness and unmercifulness. He durst not abuse the poor; for though, with his help in the gate, he could overpower them, yet he could not make his part good against that God who is the patron of oppressed poverty and will not let oppressors go unpunished (<reference osisRef="Job.31.23">v. 23</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Destruction from God was a terror to me,</hi> whenever I was tempted to this sin, and <hi type="italic">by reason of his highness I could not endure</hi> the thought of making him my enemy." He stood in awe, 1. Of the majesty of God, as a God above him. He thought of his highness, the infinite distance between him and God, which possessed him with such a reverence of him as made him very circumspect in his whole conversation. Those who oppress the poor, and pervert judgment and justice, forget that <hi type="italic">he who is higher than the highest regards,</hi> and <hi type="italic">there is a higher than they,</hi> who is able to deal with them (<reference osisRef="Eccl.5.8">Eccl. v. 8</reference>); but Job considered this. 2. Of the wrath of God, as a God that would certainly be against him if he should wrong the poor. <hi type="italic">Destruction from God,</hi> because it would be a certain and an utter ruin to him if he were guilty of this sin, was a constant terror to him, to restrain him from it. Note, Good men, even the best, have need to restrain themselves from sin with the fear of destruction from God, and all little enough. This should especially restrain us from all acts of injustice and oppression that God himself is the avenger thereof. Even when salvation from God is a comfort to us, yet destruction from God should be a terror to us. Adam, in innocency, was awed with a threatening.
entries.8e81a33eee1ba4b992a6d1042e72c3167edbe321: <div eID="gen10012" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Job's Abhorrence of Idolatry. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1520.)</title> <div sID="gen10013" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">24</hi> If I have made gold my hope, or have said to the fine gold, <hi type="italic">Thou art</hi> my confidence; <hi type="super">25</hi> If I rejoiced because my wealth <hi type="italic">was</hi> great, and because mine hand had gotten much; <hi type="super">26</hi> If I beheld the sun when it shined, or the moon walking <hi type="italic">in</hi> brightness; <hi type="super">27</hi> And my heart hath been secretly enticed, or my mouth hath kissed my hand: <hi type="super">28</hi> This also <hi type="italic">were</hi> an iniquity <hi type="italic">to be punished by</hi> the judge: for I should have denied the God <hi type="italic">that is</hi> above. 29 If I rejoiced at the destruction of him that hated me, or lifted up myself when evil found him: <hi type="super">30</hi> Neither have I suffered my mouth to sin by wishing a curse to his soul. <hi type="super">31</hi> If the men of my tabernacle said not, Oh that we had of his flesh! we cannot be satisfied. <hi type="super">32</hi> The stranger did not lodge in the street: <hi type="italic">but</hi> I opened my doors to the traveller. <div eID="gen10013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10014" type="x-p"/> Four articles more of Job's protestation we have in these verses, which, as all the rest, not only assure us what he was and did, but teach us what we should be and do:— <div eID="gen10014" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10015" type="x-p"/> I. He protests that he never set his heart upon the wealth of this world, nor took the things of it for his portions and happiness. He had gold; he had fine gold. His <hi type="italic">wealth was great,</hi> and he <hi type="italic">had gotten much.</hi> Our wealth is either advantageous or pernicious to us according as we stand affected to it. If we make it our rest and our ruler, it will be our ruin; if we make it our servant, and an instrument of righteousness, it will be a blessing to us. Job here tells us how he stood affected to his worldly wealth. 1. He put no great confidence in it: he did not <hi type="italic">make gold his hope,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.31.24">v. 24</reference>. Those are very unwise that do, and enemies to themselves, who depend upon it as sufficient to make them happy, who think themselves safe and honourable, and sure of comfort, in having abundance of this world's goods. Some make it their hope and confidence for another world, as if it were a certain token of God's favour; and those who have so much sense as not to think so yet promise themselves that it will be a portion for them in this life, whereas the things themselves are uncertain and our satisfaction in them is much more so. It is hard to have riches and not to trust in riches; and it is this which makes it so difficult for <hi type="italic">a rich man to enter into the kingdom of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.19.23">Matt. xix. 23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.10.23">Mark x. 24</reference>. 2. He took no great complacency in it (<reference osisRef="Job.31.25">v. 25</reference>): <hi type="italic">If I rejoiced because my wealth was great</hi> and boasted that <hi type="italic">my hand had gotten much.</hi> He took no pride in his wealth, as if it added any thing to his real excellency, nor did he think that his might and the power of his hand obtained it for him, <reference osisRef="Deut.8.17">Deut. viii. 17</reference>. He took no pleasure in it in comparison with the spiritual things which were the delight of his soul. His joy did not terminate in the gift, but passed through it to the giver. When he was in the midst of his abundance he never said, <hi type="italic">Soul, take thy ease</hi> in these things, <hi type="italic">eat, drink, and be merry,</hi> nor blessed himself in his riches. He did not inordinately rejoice in his wealth, which helped him to bear the loss of it so patiently as he did. The way to <hi type="italic">weep as though we wept not</hi> is to <hi type="italic">rejoice as though we rejoiced not.</hi> The less pleasure the enjoyment is the less pain the disappointment will be. <div eID="gen10015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10016" type="x-p"/> II. He protests that he never gave the worship and glory to the creature which are due to God only; he was never guilty of idolatry, <reference osisRef="Job.31.26-Job.31.28">v. 26-28</reference>. We do not find that Job's friends charged him with this. But there were those, it seems, at that time, who were so sottish as to worship the sun and moon, else Job would not have mentioned it. Idolatry is one of the old ways which wicked men have trodden, and the most ancient idolatry was the worshipping of the sun and moon, to which the temptation was most strong, as appears <reference osisRef="Deut.4.19">Deut. iv. 19</reference>, where Moses speaks of the danger which the people were in of being driven to worship them. But as yet it was practised secretly, and durst not appear in open view, as afterwards the most abominable idolatries did. Observe, <div eID="gen10016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10017" type="x-p"/> 1. How far Job kept from this sin. He not only never bowed the knee to Baal (which, some think, was designed to represent the sun), never fell down and worshipped the sun, but he kept his eye, his heart, and his lips, clean from this sin. (1.) He never so much as beheld the sun or the moon in their pomp and lustre with any other admiration of them than what led him to give all the glory of their brightness and usefulness to their Creator. Against spiritual as well as corporal adultery he made a covenant with his eyes; and this was his covenant, that, whenever he looked at the lights of heaven, he should by faith look through them, and beyond them, to the Father of lights. (2.) He kept his heart with all diligence, that that should not be secretly enticed to think that there is a divine glory in their brightness, or a divine power in their influence, and that therefore divine honours are to be paid to them. Here is the source of idolatry; it begins in the heart. Every man is tempted to that, as to other sins, when he is <hi type="italic">drawn away by his own lust and enticed.</hi> (3.) He did not so much as put a compliment upon these pretended deities, did not perform the least and lowest act of adoration: <hi type="italic">His mouth did not kiss his hand,</hi> which, it is likely, was a ceremony then commonly used even by some that yet would not be thought idolaters. It is an old-fashioned piece of civil respect among ourselves, in making a bow, to kiss the hand, a form which, it seems, was anciently used in giving divine honours to the sun and moon. They could not reach to kiss them, as <hi type="italic">the men that sacrificed kissed the calves</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hos.13.2">Hos. xiii. 2</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.19.18">1 Kings xix. 18</reference>); but, to show their good will, they kissed their hand, reverencing those as their masters which God has made servants to this lower world, to hold the candle for us. Job never did it. <div eID="gen10017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10018" type="x-p"/> 2. How ill Job thought of this sin, <reference osisRef="Job.31.28">v. 28</reference>. (1.) He looked upon it as an affront to the civil magistrate: It <hi type="italic">were an iniquity to be punished by the judge,</hi> as a public nuisance, and hurtful to kings and provinces. Idolatry debauches men's minds, corrupts their manners, takes off the true sense of religion which is the great bond of societies, and provokes God to give men up to a reprobate sense, and to send judgments upon a nation; and therefore the conservators of the public peace are concerned to restrain it by punishing it. (2.) He looked upon it as a much greater affront to the God of heaven, and no less than high treason against his crown and dignity: For <hi type="italic">I should have denied the God that is above,</hi> denied his being as God and his sovereignty as God above. Idolatry is, in effect, atheism; hence the Gentiles are said to be <hi type="italic">without God (atheists) in the world.</hi> Note, We should be afraid of every thing that does but tacitly deny the God above, his providence, or any of his perfections. <div eID="gen10018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10019" type="x-p"/> III. He protests that he was so far from doing or designing mischief to any that he neither desired nor delighted in the hurt of the worst enemy he had. The forgiving of those that do us evil, it seems, was Old-Testament duty, though the Pharisees made the law concerning it of no effect, by teaching, <hi type="italic">Thou shalt love thy neighbour and hate thy enemy,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.5.43">Matt. v. 43</reference>. Observe here, <div eID="gen10019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10020" type="x-p"/> 1. Job was far from revenge. He did not only not return the injuries that were done him, not only not destroy those who hated him; but, (1.) He did not so much as rejoice when any mischief befel them, <reference osisRef="Job.31.29">v. 29</reference>. Many who would not wilfully hurt those who stand in their light, or have done them a diskindness, yet are secretly pleased and laugh in their sleeve (as we say) when hurt is done them. But Job was not of that spirit. Though Job was a very good man, yet, it seems, there were those that hated him; but evil found them. He saw their destruction, and was far from rejoicing in it; for that would justly have brought the destruction upon him, as it is intimated, <reference osisRef="Prov.24.17-Prov.24.18">Prov. xxiv. 17, 18</reference>. (2.) He did not so much as wish in his own mind that evil might befel them, <reference osisRef="Job.31.30">v. 30</reference>. He never <hi type="italic">wished a curse to his soul</hi> (curses to the soul are the worst of curses), never desired his death; he knew that, if he did, it would turn into sin to him. He was careful <hi type="italic">not to offend with his tongue</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.39.1">Ps. xxxix. 1</reference>), would not <hi type="italic">suffer his mouth to sin,</hi> and therefore durst not imprecate any evil, no, not to his worst enemy. If others bear malice to us, that will not justify us in bearing malice to them. <div eID="gen10020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10021" type="x-p"/> 2. He was violently urged to revenge, and yet he kept himself thus clear from it (<reference osisRef="Job.31.31">v. 31</reference>): <hi type="italic">The men of his tabernacle,</hi> his domestics, his servants, and those about him, were so enraged at Job's enemy who hated him, that they could have eaten him, if Job would but have set them on or given them leave. "<hi type="italic">O that we had of his flesh!</hi> Our master is satisfied to forgive him, but <hi type="italic">we cannot be so satisfied.</hi>" See how much beloved Job was by his family, how heartily they espoused his cause, and what enemies they were to his enemies; but see what a strict hand Job kept upon his passions, that he would not avenge himself, though he had those about him that blew the coals of his resentment. Note, (1.) A good man commonly does not himself lay to heart the affronts that are done him so much as his friends do for him. (2.) Great men have commonly those about them that stir them up to revenge. David had so, <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.4">1 Sam. xxiv. 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.8">xxvi. 8</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.9">2 Sam. xvi. 9</reference>. But if they keep their temper, notwithstanding the spiteful insinuations of those about them, afterwards it shall be no grief of heart to them, but shall turn very much to their praise. <div eID="gen10021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10022" type="x-p"/> IV. He protests that he had never been unkind or inhospitable to strangers (<reference osisRef="Job.31.32">v. 32</reference>): <hi type="italic">The stranger lodged not in the street,</hi> as angels might lately have done in the streets of Sodom if Lot alone had not entertained them. Perhaps by that instance Job was taught (as we are, <reference osisRef="Heb.13.2">Heb. xiii. 2</reference>) not to be forgetful to entertain strangers. He that is at home must consider those that are from home, and put his soul into their soul's stead, and then do as he would be done by. Hospitality is a Christian duty, <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.9">1 Pet. iv. 9</reference>. Job, in his prosperity, was noted for good house-keeping: <hi type="italic">He opened his door to the road</hi> (so it may be read); he kept the street-door open, that he might see who passed by and invite them in, as Abraham, <reference osisRef="Gen.18.1">Gen. xviii. 1</reference>.
entries.cadd2a03a08141ec756c8a31fcc4828c5faaabe3: <div eID="gen10022" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Job's Protestation of His Integrity. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1520.)</title> <div sID="gen10023" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">33</hi> If I covered my transgressions as Adam, by hiding mine iniquity in my bosom: <hi type="super">34</hi> Did I fear a great multitude, or did the contempt of families terrify me, that I kept silence, <hi type="italic">and</hi> went not out of the door? <hi type="super">35</hi> Oh that one would hear me! behold, my desire <hi type="italic">is, that</hi> the Almighty would answer me, and <hi type="italic">that</hi> mine adversary had written a book. 36 Surely I would take it upon my shoulder, <hi type="italic">and</hi> bind it <hi type="italic">as</hi> a crown to me. <hi type="super">37</hi> I would declare unto him the number of my steps; as a prince would I go near unto him. <hi type="super">38</hi> If my land cry against me, or that the furrows likewise thereof complain; <hi type="super">39</hi> If I have eaten the fruits thereof without money, or have caused the owners thereof to lose their life: <hi type="super">40</hi> Let thistles grow instead of wheat, and cockle instead of barley. The words of Job are ended. <div eID="gen10023" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10024" type="x-p"/> We have here Job's protestation against three more sins, together with his general appeal to God's bar and his petition for a hearing there, which, it is likely, was intended to conclude his discourse (and therefore we will consider it last), but that another particular sin occurred, from which he thought it requisite to acquit himself. He clears himself from the charge, <div eID="gen10024" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10025" type="x-p"/> I. Of dissimulation and hypocrisy. The general crime of which his friends accused him was that, under the cloak of a profession of religion, he had kept up secret haunts of sin, and that really he was as bad as other people, but had the art of concealing it. Zophar insinuated (<reference osisRef="Job.20.12">ch. xx. 12</reference>) that he <hi type="italic">hid his iniquity under his tongue.</hi> "No," says Job, "I never did (<reference osisRef="Job.31.33">v. 33</reference>), <hi type="italic">I never covered my transgression as Adam,</hi> never palliated a sin with frivolous excuses, nor made fig-leaves the shelter of my shame, nor ever <hi type="italic">hid my iniquity in my bosom,</hi> as a fondling, a darling, that I could by no means part with, or as stolen goods which I dreaded the discovery of." It is natural to us to cover our sins; we have it from our first parents. We are loth to confess our faults, willing to extenuate them and make the best of ourselves, to devolve the blame upon others, as Adam on his wife, not without a tacit reflection upon God himself. But <hi type="italic">he that</hi> thus <hi type="italic">covers his sins shall not prosper,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.28.13">Prov. xxviii. 13</reference>. Job, in this protestation, intimates two things, which were certain evidences of his integrity:—1. That he was not guilty of any great transgression or iniquity, inconsistent with sincerity, which he had now industriously concealed. In this protestation he had dealt fairly, and, while he denies some sins, was not conscious to himself that he allowed himself in any. 2. That what transgression and iniquity he had been guilty of (<hi type="italic">Who is there that lives and sins not?</hi>) he had always been ready to own it, and, as soon as ever he perceived he had said or done amiss, he was ready to unsay it and undo it, as far as he could, by repentance, confessing it both to God and man, and forsaking it: this is doing honestly. <div eID="gen10025" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10026" type="x-p"/> II. From the charge of cowardice and base fear. His courage in that which is good he produces as an evidence of his sincerity in it (<reference osisRef="Job.31.34">v. 34</reference>): <hi type="italic">Did I fear a great multitude, that I kept silence?</hi> No, all that knew Job knew him to be a man of undaunted resolution in a good cause, that boldly appeared, spoke, and acted, in defence of religion and justice, and did not fear the face of man nor was ever threatened or brow-beaten out of his duty, but set his face as a flint. Observe, 1. What great conscience Job had made of his duty as a magistrate, or a man of reputation, in the place where he lived. He did not, he durst not, keep silence when he had a call to speak in an honest cause, or keep within doors when he had a call to go abroad to do good. The case may be such that it may be our sin to be silent and retired, as when we are called to reprove sin and bear our testimony against it, to vindicate the truths and ways of God, to do justice to those who are injured or oppressed, or in any way to serve the public or to do honour to our religion. 2. What little account Job made of the discouragements he met with in the way of his duty. He valued not the clamours of the mob, feared not a great multitude, nor did he value the menaces of the mighty: <hi type="italic">The contempt of families never terrified him.</hi> He was not deterred by the number or quality, the scorns or insults, or the injurious from doing justice to the injured; no, he scorned to be swayed and biassed by any such considerations, nor ever suffered a righteous cause to be run down by a high hand. He feared the great God, not the multitude, and his curse, not the contempt of families. <div eID="gen10026" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10027" type="x-p"/> III. From the charge of oppression and violence, and doing wrong to his poor neighbours. And here observe, <div eID="gen10027" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10028" type="x-p"/> 1. What his protestation is—that the estate he had he both got and used honestly, so that his <hi type="italic">land</hi> could not <hi type="italic">cry out against him nor the furrows thereof complain</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.31.38">v. 38</reference>), as they do against those who get the possession of them by fraud and extortion, <reference osisRef="Hab.2.9-Hab.2.11">Hab. ii. 9-11</reference>. The whole creation is said to groan under the sin of man; but that which is unjustly gained and held cries out against a man, and accuses him, condemns him, and demands justice against him for the injury. Rather than his oppression shall go unpunished the very ground and the furrows of it shall witness against him, and be his prosecutors. Two things he could say safely concerning his estate:—(1.) That he <hi type="italic">never ate the fruits of it without money,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.31.39">v. 39</reference>. What he purchased he paid for, as Abraham for the land he bought (<reference osisRef="Gen.23.16">Gen. xxiii. 16</reference>), and David, <reference osisRef="2Sam.24.24">2 Sam. xxiv. 24</reference>. The labourers that he employed had their wages duly paid them, and, if he made use of the fruits of those lands that he let out, he paid his tenants for them, or allowed it in their rent. (2.) That he never caused the owners thereof to lose their life, never got an estate, as Ahab got Naboth's vineyard, by killing the heir and seizing the inheritance, never starved those that held lands of him nor killed them with hard bargains and hard usage. No tenant, no workman, no servant, he had, could complain of him. <div eID="gen10028" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10029" type="x-p"/> 2. How he confirms his protestation. He does it, as often before, with a suitable imprecation (<reference osisRef="Job.31.40">v. 40</reference>): "If I have got my estate unjustly, <hi type="italic">let thistles grow instead of wheat,</hi> the worst of weeds instead of the best of grains." When men get estates unjustly they are justly deprived of the comfort of them, and disappointed in their expectations from them. They sow their land, but they sow not that body that shall be. God will give it a body. It was sown wheat, but shall come up thistles. What men do not come honestly by will never do them any good. Job, towards the close of his protestation, appeals to the judgment-seat of God concerning the truth of it (<reference osisRef="Job.31.35-Job.31.37">v. 35-37</reference>): <hi type="italic">O that he would hear me,</hi> even <hi type="italic">that the Almighty would answer me!</hi> This was what he desired and often complained that he could not obtain; and, now that he had drawn up his own defence so particularly, he leaves it upon record, in expectation of a hearing, files it, as it were, till his cause be called. <div eID="gen10029" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10030" type="x-p"/> (1.) A trial is moved for, and the motion earnestly pressed: "<hi type="italic">O that one,</hi> any one, <hi type="italic">would hear me;</hi> my cause is so good, and my evidence so clear, that I am willing to refer it to any indifferent person whatsoever; but my desire is that the Almighty himself would determine it." An upright heart does not dread a scrutiny. He that means honestly wishes he had a window in his breast, that all men might see the intents of his heart. But an upright heart does particularly desire to be determined in every thing by the judgment of God, which we are sure is according to the truth. It was holy David's prayer, <hi type="italic">Search me, O God! and know my heart;</hi> and it was blessed Paul's comfort, <hi type="italic">He that judgeth me is the Lord.</hi> <div eID="gen10030" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10031" type="x-p"/> (2.) The prosecutor is called, the plaintiff summoned, and ordered to bring in his information, to say what he has to say against the prisoner, for he stands upon his deliverance: "<hi type="italic">O that my adversary had written a book</hi>—that my friends, who charge me with hypocrisy, would draw up their charge in writing, that it might be reduced to a certainty, and that we might the better join issue upon it." Job would be very glad to see the libel, to have a copy of his indictment. He would not hide it under his arm, but <hi type="italic">take it upon his shoulder,</hi> to be seen and read of all men, nay, he would <hi type="italic">bind it as a crown</hi> to him, would be pleased with it, and look upon it as his ornament; for, [1.] If it discovered to him any sin he had been guilty of, which he did not yet see, he should be glad to know it, that he might repent of it and get it pardoned. A good man is willing to know the worst of himself and will be thankful to those that will faithfully tell him of his faults. [2.] If it charged him with what was false, he doubted not but to disprove the allegations, that his innocency would be cleared up as the light, and he should come off with so much the more honour. But, [3.] He believed that, when his adversaries came to consider the matter so closely as they must do if they put the charge in writing, the accusations would be trivial and minute, and every one that saw them would say, "If this was all they had to say against him, it was a shame they gave him so much trouble." <div eID="gen10031" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10032" type="x-p"/> (3.) The defendant is ready to make his appearance and to give his accusers all the fair play they can desire. He will <hi type="italic">declare unto them the number of his steps,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.31.37">v. 37</reference>. He will let them into the history of his own life, will show them all the stages and scenes of it. He will give them a narrative of his conversation, what would make against him as well as what would make for him, and let them make what use they pleased of it; and so confident he is of his integrity that as a prince to be crowned, rather than a prisoner to be tried, he would <hi type="italic">go near to him,</hi> both to his accuser to hear his charge and to his judge to hear his doom. Thus the testimony of his conscience was his rejoicing. <div eID="gen10032" type="x-p"/> <lg sID="gen10033"/> <l level="1" sID="gen10034"/>Hic murus aheneus esto, nil conscire sibi—<l eID="gen10034" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen10035"/>Be this thy brazen bulwark of defence,<l eID="gen10035" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen10036"/>Still to preserve thy conscience innocence.<l eID="gen10036" level="1"/> <lg eID="gen10033"/> <div sID="gen10037" type="x-p"/> Those that have kept their hands without spot from the world, as Job did, may lift up their faces without spot unto God, and may comfort themselves with the prospect of his judgment when they lie under the unjust censures of men. <hi type="italic">If our hearts condemn us not, then have we confidence towards God.</hi> <div eID="gen10037" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10038" type="x-p"/> Thus <hi type="italic">the words of Job are ended;</hi> that is, he has now said all he would say in answer to his friends: he afterwards said something in a way of self-reproach and condemnation (<reference osisRef="Job.40.4-Job.40.5">ch. xl. 4, 5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.42.2-Job.42.6">xlii. 2</reference>, &c.), but here ends what he had to say in a way of self-defence and vindication. If this suffice not he will say no more; he knows when he has said enough and will submit to the judgment of the bench. Some think the manner of expression intimates that he concluded with an air of assurance and triumph. He now keeps the field and doubts not but to win the field. <hi type="italic">Who shall lay any thing to the charge of God's elect? It is God that justifies.</hi>  <chapter eID="Job.31"/> <div eID="gen10038" type="x-p"/>

entries.845af24f971ddf56af73d6246febfac80fe4779a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5122"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 31</title> <div sID="gen7616" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Job.31.1-Job.31.40">Job 31:1-40</reference>.<div eID="gen7616" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7617" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5122"/>1. Job proceeds to prove that he deserved a better lot. As in the twenty-ninth chapter, he showed his uprightness as an emir, or magistrate in public life, so in this chapter he vindicates his character in private life. <div eID="gen7617" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5123"/><div sID="gen7618" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5123"/>1-4. He asserts his guarding against being allured to sin by his senses.<div eID="gen7618" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7619" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">think--</hi>rather, "cast a (lustful) look." He not merely did not so, but put it out of the question by covenanting with his eyes against leading him into temptation (<reference osisRef="Prov.6.25">Pr 6:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.5.28">Mt 5:28</reference>). <div eID="gen7619" type="x-p"/>
entries.395c08358dfde48907a7bfd3a548c004e8ab8297: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5127"/><div sID="gen7624" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5127"/>5. Job's abstinence from evil deeds.<div eID="gen7624" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7625" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">vanity--</hi>that is, falsehood (<reference osisRef="Ps.12.2">Psa 12:2</reference>). <div eID="gen7625" type="x-p"/>
entries.df9fd7dd68ba9f12b14677a6b1d7065c1eb25c9e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5128"/><div sID="gen7626" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5128"/>6. Parenthetical. Translate: "Oh, that God would weigh me ... then would He know," &c. <div eID="gen7626" type="x-p"/>
entries.c65f4240e45ac39abebf2f646aa546c493205c7f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5129"/><div sID="gen7627" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5129"/>7. Connected with <reference osisRef="Job.31.6">Job 31:6</reference>.<div eID="gen7627" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7628" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the way--</hi>of God (<reference osisRef="Job.23.11">Job 23:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.5.5">Jr 5:5</reference>). A godly life.<div eID="gen7628" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7629" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">heart ... after ... eyes--</hi>if my heart coveted, what my eyes beheld (<reference osisRef="Eccl.11.9">Ec 11:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.7.21">Jos 7:21</reference>).<div eID="gen7629" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7630" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hands--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.24.4">Psa 24:4</reference>). <div eID="gen7630" type="x-p"/>
entries.e5bb606dba35fcb076d2fc2beae44b144a32aa13: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5130"/><div sID="gen7631" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5130"/>8. Apodosis to <reference osisRef="Job.31.5">Job 31:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.31.7">7</reference>; the curses which he imprecates on himself, if he had done these things (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.16">Le 26:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.9.14">Am 9:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.128.2">Psa 128:2</reference>).<div eID="gen7631" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7632" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">offspring--</hi>rather, "what I plant," my harvests. <div eID="gen7632" type="x-p"/>
entries.d669aaf09e241f0a45a5c5ef7493834a2f7efe1a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5131"/><div sID="gen7633" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5131"/>9-12. Job asserts his innocence of adultery.<div eID="gen7633" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7634" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">deceived--</hi>hath let itself be seduced (<reference osisRef="Prov.7.8">Pr 7:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.39.7-Gen.39.12">Ge 39:7-12</reference>).<div eID="gen7634" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7635" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">laid wait--</hi>until the husband went out. <div eID="gen7635" type="x-p"/>
entries.5f72e1fa0e0a6ba88c7ed1d5231616b258796cd4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5135"/><div sID="gen7639" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5135"/>13-23. Job affirms his freedom from unfairness towards his servants, from harshness and oppression towards the needy.<div eID="gen7639" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7640" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">despise the cause--</hi>refused to do them justice. <div eID="gen7640" type="x-p"/>
entries.ea6c545231be644ee72bae473a37e0e908ab5897: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5146"/><div sID="gen7657" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5146"/>24-25. Job asserts his freedom from trust in money (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.17">1Ti 6:17</reference>). Here he turns to his duty towards God, as before he had spoken of his duty towards himself and his neighbor. Covetousness is covert idolatry, as it transfers the heart from the Creator to the creature (<reference osisRef="Col.3.5">Col 3:5</reference>). In <reference osisRef="Job.31.26">Job 31:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.31.27">27</reference> he passes to overt idolatry. <div eID="gen7657" type="x-p"/>
entries.33dc00a0170699a7d0eb406fde72f564b5271d32: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5147"/><div sID="gen7658" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5147"/>26. If I looked unto the sun (as an object of worship) because he shined; or to the moon because she walked, &c. Sabaism (from tsaba, "the heavenly hosts") was the earliest form of false worship. God is hence called in contradistinction, "Lord of Sabaoth." The sun, moon, and stars, the brightest objects in nature, and seen everywhere, were supposed to be visible representatives of the invisible God. They had no temples, but were worshipped on high places and roofs of houses (<reference osisRef="Ezek.8.16">Eze 8:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.4.19">De 4:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.5">2Ki 23:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.11">11</reference>). The Hebrew here for "sun" is light. Probably light was worshipped as the emanation from God, before its embodiments, the sun, &c. This worship prevailed in Chaldea; wherefore Job's exemption from the idolatry of his neighbors was the more exemplary. Our "Sun-day," "Mon-day," or Moon-day, bear traces of Sabaism. <div eID="gen7658" type="x-p"/>
entries.e96b5747d50f7700298b140b87c4bcb29358f94a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5148"/><div sID="gen7659" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5148"/><hi type="bold">27. enticed--</hi>away from God to idolatry.<div eID="gen7659" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7660" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">kissed ... hand--</hi>"adoration," literally means this. In worshipping they used to kiss the hand, and then throw the kiss, as it were, towards the object of worship (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.19.18">1Ki 19:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.13.2">Ho 13:2</reference>). <div eID="gen7660" type="x-p"/>
entries.72c169c0e2fcd4a79827839e1cf54aa05d17686a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5149"/><div sID="gen7661" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5149"/>28. The Mosaic law embodied subsequently the feeling of the godly from the earliest times against idolatry, as deserving judicial penalties: being treason against the Supreme King (<reference osisRef="Deut.13.9">De 13:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.17.2-Deut.17.7">17:2-7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.8.14-Ezek.8.18">Eze 8:14-18</reference>). This passage therefore does not prove Job to have been subsequent to Moses. <div eID="gen7661" type="x-p"/>
entries.57d127fb0cf59bc09f3fec2d5e74ef0b3b10f7b2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5150"/><div sID="gen7662" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5150"/><hi type="bold">29. lifted up myself--</hi>in malicious triumph (<reference osisRef="Prov.17.5">Pr 17:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.24.17">24:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.7.4">Psa 7:4</reference>). <div eID="gen7662" type="x-p"/>
entries.6b32c0743768a2e0ce0002fbf913c637edfe010c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5151"/><div sID="gen7663" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5151"/><hi type="bold">30. mouth--</hi>literally, "palate." (See on <reference osisRef="Job.6.30">Job 6:30</reference>).<div eID="gen7663" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7664" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wishing--</hi>literally, "so as to demand his (my enemy's) soul," that is, "life by a curse." This verse parenthetically confirms <reference osisRef="Job.31.30">Job 31:30</reference>. Job in the patriarchal age of the promise, anterior to the law, realizes the Gospel spirit, which was the end of the law (compare <reference osisRef="Lev.19.18">Le 19:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.23.6">De 23:6</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Matt.5.43">Mt 5:43</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.44">44</reference>). <div eID="gen7664" type="x-p"/>
entries.ac5f738fdee5ce69440068ffcb52686f1224d1c3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5152"/><div sID="gen7665" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5152"/>31. That is, Job's household said, Oh, that we had Job's enemy to devour, we cannot rest satisfied till we have! But Job refrained from even wishing revenge (<reference osisRef="1Sam.26.8">1Sa 26:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.9">2Sa 16:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.10">10</reference>). So Jesus Christ (<reference osisRef="Luke.9.54">Lu 9:54</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.9.55">55</reference>). But, better (see <reference osisRef="Job.31.32">Job 31:32</reference>), translated, "Who can show (literally, give) the man who was not satisfied with the flesh (meat) provided by Job?" He never let a poor man leave his gate without giving him enough to eat. <div eID="gen7665" type="x-p"/>
entries.bc8423afa4ef8e735d96cb2db00b76b8cb21a69e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5153"/><div sID="gen7666" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5153"/><hi type="bold">32. traveller--</hi>literally, "way," that is, wayfarers; so expressed to include all of every kind (<reference osisRef="2Sam.12.4">2Sa 12:4</reference>). <div eID="gen7666" type="x-p"/>
entries.2e9299cf1be258a07ee0f81bec9e4237123c039b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5154"/><div sID="gen7667" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5154"/><hi type="bold">33. Adam--</hi>translated by Umbreit, "as men do" (<reference osisRef="Hos.6.7">Ho 6:7</reference>, where see Margin). But English Version is more natural. The very same word for "hiding" is used in <reference osisRef="Gen.3.8">Ge 3:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.3.10">10</reference>, of Adam hiding himself from God. Job elsewhere alludes to the flood. So he might easily know of the fall, through the two links which connect Adam and Abraham (about Job's time), namely, Methuselah and Shem. Adam is representative of fallen man's propensity to concealment (<reference osisRef="Prov.28.13">Pr 28:13</reference>). It was from God that Job did not "hide his iniquity in his bosom," as on the contrary it was from God that "Adam" hid in his lurking-place. This disproves the translation, "as men"; for it is from their fellow men that "men" are chiefly anxious to hide their real character as guilty. Magee, to make the comparison with Adam more exact, for my "bosom" translates, "lurking-place." <div eID="gen7667" type="x-p"/>
entries.35462db030f2d9d1ffaf6f23529377fc7c285ed5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5155"/><div sID="gen7668" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5155"/><hi type="bold">34. Rather, the apodosis to <reference osisRef="Job.31.33">Job 31:33</reference>, "Then let me be fear-stricken before a great multitude, let the contempt, &c., let me keep silence (the greatest disgrace to a patriot, heretofore so prominent in assemblies), and not go out," &c. A just retribution that he who hides his sin from God, should have it exposed before man (<reference osisRef="2Sam.12.12">2Sa 12:12</reference>). But Job had not been so exposed, but on the contrary was esteemed in the assemblies of the "tribes"--</hi>("families"); a proof, he implies, that God does not hold him guilty of hiding sin (<reference osisRef="Job.24.16">Job 24:16</reference>, contrast with <reference osisRef="Job.29.21-Job.29.25">Job 29:21-25</reference>). <div eID="gen7668" type="x-p"/>
entries.19995a84b86c161f00e0648f7f8bc8df554f629e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5156"/><div sID="gen7669" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5156"/>35. Job returns to his wish (<reference osisRef="Job.13.22">Job 13:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.19.23">19:23</reference>). Omit "is"; "Behold my sign," that is, my mark of subscription to the statements just given in my defense: the mark of signature was originally a cross; and hence the letter Tau or T. Translate, also "Oh, that the Almighty," &c. He marks "God" as the "One" meant in the first clause.<div eID="gen7669" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7670" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">adversary--</hi>that is, he who contends with me, refers also to God. The vagueness is designed to express "whoever it be that judicially opposes me"--the Almighty if it be He.<div eID="gen7670" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7671" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">had written a book--</hi>rather, "would write down his charge." <div eID="gen7671" type="x-p"/>
entries.2d8c61bb6991839cf49684c4c3f8c2bc91e20ebe: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5157"/><div sID="gen7672" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5157"/>36. So far from hiding the adversary's "answer" or "charge" through fear,<div eID="gen7672" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7673" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I would take it on my shoulders--</hi>as a public honor (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.6">Is 9:6</reference>).<div eID="gen7673" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7674" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">a crown--</hi>not a mark of shame, but of distinction (<reference osisRef="Isa.62.3">Is 62:3</reference>). <div eID="gen7674" type="x-p"/>
entries.fbd1172b71a70db508dd152e84b3bf7bcc204d02: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5158"/><div sID="gen7675" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5158"/>37. A good conscience imparts a princely dignity before man and free assurance in approaching God. This can be realized, not in Job's way (<reference osisRef="Job.42.5">Job 42:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.42.6">6</reference>); but only through Jesus Christ (<reference osisRef="Heb.10.22">He 10:22</reference>). <div eID="gen7675" type="x-p"/>
entries.203b21b66d7eb1b1e25c5236c6b7dc002fcfdaeb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5159"/><div sID="gen7676" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5159"/>38. Personification. The complaints of the unjustly ousted proprietors are transferred to the lands themselves (<reference osisRef="Job.31.20">Job 31:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.4.10">Ge 4:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.2.11">Ha 2:11</reference>). If I have unjustly acquired lands (<reference osisRef="Job.24.2">Job 24:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.5.8">Is 5:8</reference>).<div eID="gen7676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7677" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">furrows--</hi>The specification of these makes it likely, he implies in this, "If I paid not the laborer for tillage"; as <reference osisRef="Job.31.39">Job 31:39</reference>, "If I paid him not for gathering in the fruits." Thus of the four clauses in <reference osisRef="Job.31.38">Job 31:38</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.31.39">39</reference>, the first refers to the same subject as the fourth, the second is connected with the third by introverted parallelism.
