Compare <reference osisRef="Jas.5.4">Jas 5:4</reference>, which plainly alludes to this passage: compare "Lord of Sabaoth" with <reference osisRef="Job.31.26">Job 31:26</reference> here. <div eID="gen7677" type="x-p"/>
entries.328a76ef3f4fe78ecc8029a75b00ed0274f723f6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5160"/><div sID="gen7678" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5160"/><hi type="bold">39. lose ... life--</hi>not literally, but "harassed to death"; until he gave me up his land gratis [Maurer]; as in <reference osisRef="Judg.16.16">Jud 16:16</reference>; "suffered him to languish" by taking away his means of living [Umbreit] (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.21.19">1Ki 21:19</reference>). <div eID="gen7678" type="x-p"/>
entries.17fbf7afc1b54f63f1811e381e03220ed9aa8fed: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5161"/><div sID="gen7679" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5161"/><hi type="bold">40. thistles--</hi>or brambles, thorns.<div eID="gen7679" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7680" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cockle--</hi>literally, "noxious weeds."<div eID="gen7680" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7681" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">The words ... ended--</hi>that is, in the controversy with the friends. He spoke in the book afterwards, but not to them. At <reference osisRef="Job.31.37">Job 31:37</reference> would be the regular conclusion in strict art. But <reference osisRef="Job.31.38-Job.31.40">Job 31:38-40</reference> are naturally added by one whose mind in agitation recurs to its sense of innocence, even after it has come to the usual stopping point; this takes away the appearance of rhetorical artifice. Hence the transposition by Eichorn of <reference osisRef="Job.31.38-Job.31.40">Job 31:38-40</reference> to follow <reference osisRef="Job.31.25">Job 31:25</reference> is quite unwarranted. <chapter eID="Job.31"/>

entries.573e310fc0c061478202b4126b22d113a7ef253d: <div eID="gen17412" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen17413" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen17414" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen17414" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen17413" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen17415" type="x-p"/> Job makes a solemn protestation of his chastity and integrity, <reference osisRef="Job.31.1-Job.31.12">Job 31:1-12</reference>; of his humanity, <reference osisRef="Job.31.13-Job.31.16">Job 31:13-16</reference>; of his charity and mercy, <reference osisRef="Job.31.17-Job.31.23">Job 31:17-23</reference>; of his abhorrence of covetousness and idolatry, <reference osisRef="Job.31.24-Job.31.32">Job 31:24-32</reference>; and of his readiness to acknowledge his errors, <reference osisRef="Job.31.33">Job 31:33</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.31.34">Job 31:34</reference>; and wishes for a full investigation of his case, being confident that this would issue in the full manifestation of his innocence, <reference osisRef="Job.31.36-Job.31.40">Job 31:36-40</reference>. <div eID="gen17415" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17416" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen17416" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17417" type="x-p"/> I made a covenant with mine eyes - ברית כרתי לעיני berith carati leeynai: "I have cut" or divided "the covenant sacrifice with my eyes." My conscience and my eyes are the contracting parties; God is the Judge; and I am therefore bound not to look upon any thing with a delighted or covetous eye, by which my conscience may be defiled, or my God dishonored. <div eID="gen17417" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17418" type="x-p"/> Why then should I think upon a maid? - ומה אתבונן על בתולה umah ethbonen al bethulah. And why should I set myself to contemplate, or think upon, Bethulah? That Bethulah may here signify an idol, is very likely. Sanchoniatho observes, that Ouranos first introduced Baithulia when he erected animated stones, or rather, as Bochart observes, Anointed stones, which became representatives of some deity. I suppose that Job purges himself here from this species of idolatry. Probably the Baithulia were at first emblems only of the tabernacle; בית אלוה beith Eloah, "the house of God;" or of that pillar set up by Jacob, <reference osisRef="Gen.28.18">Gen 28:18</reference>, which he called בית אלהים beith Elohim, or Bethalim; for idolatry always supposes a pure and holy worship, of which it is the counterfeit. For more on the subject of the Baithulia, see the notes on <reference osisRef="Gen.28.19">Gen 28:19</reference>.
entries.82cd75397866d97d2aba166b60882a0cf967d2a6: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen17418" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17419" type="x-p"/> For what portion of God is there from above? - Though I have not, in this or in any other respect, wickedly departed from God, yet what reward have I received?
entries.7f714c57cff33a261b9677b1f7e66c5987f42e7e: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen17419" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17420" type="x-p"/> Is not destruction to the wicked - If I had been guilty of such secret hypocritical proceedings, professing faith in the true God while in eye and heart an idolater, would not such a worker of iniquity be distinguished by a strange and unheard-of punishment?
entries.b779f535ffa10813a42f0a24e07855bf4088d284: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen17420" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17421" type="x-p"/> Doth not he see my ways - Can I suppose that I could screen myself from the eye of God while guilty of such iniquities?
entries.549f4b7406e7106b4cdc85bc6bc6c02da761bdbf: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen17421" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17422" type="x-p"/> If I have walked with vanity - If I have been guilty of idolatry, or the worshipping of a false god: for thus שאו shau, which we here translate vanity, is used <reference osisRef="Jer.18.15">Jer 18:15</reference>; (compare with <reference osisRef="Psa.31.6">Psa 31:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.12.11">Hos 12:11</reference>; and <reference osisRef="Jon.2.9">Jon 2:9</reference>), and it seems evident that the whole of Job's discourse here is a vindication of himself from all idolatrous dispositions and practices.
entries.dbccdd8158d2b1c5ea4ae73076171342fa578822: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen17422" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17423" type="x-p"/> Mine integrity - תמתי tummathi, my perfection; the totality of my unblameable life.
entries.59a5ef31a521525565075cd2ec24302bf456e0d5: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen17423" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17424" type="x-p"/> If my step hath turned out of the way - I am willing to be sifted to the uttermost - for every step of my foot, for every thought of my heart, for every look of mine eye, and for every act of my hands.
entries.a3ffb29076fa59bce75c82c746b889c00e3352f9: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen17424" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17425" type="x-p"/> Let me sow, and let another eat - Let me be plagued both in my circumstances and in my family. <div eID="gen17425" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17426" type="x-p"/> My offspring be rooted out - It has already appeared probable that all Job's children were not destroyed in the fall of the house mentioned <reference osisRef="Job.1.18">Job 1:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.1.19">Job 1:19</reference>.
entries.5f3061958e603e64f6f4981925953905f67282f4: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen17426" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17427" type="x-p"/> If mine heart have been deceived by a woman - The Septuagint add, ανδρος ἑτερου, another man's wife.
entries.b5b7a7eb04a4a0115dcfc164a16763073b6c43e6: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen17427" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17428" type="x-p"/> Let my wife grind unto another - Let her work at the handmill, grinding corn; which was the severe work of the meanest slave. In this sense the passage is understood both by the Syriac and Arabic. See <reference osisRef="Exo.11.5">Exo 11:5</reference> (note), and <reference osisRef="Isa.47.2">Isa 47:2</reference> (note); and see at the end of the chapter, <reference osisRef="Isa.31.8">Isa 31:8</reference> (note). <div eID="gen17428" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17429" type="x-p"/> And let others bow down upon her - Let her be in such a state as to have no command of her own person; her owner disposing of her person as he pleases. In Asiatic countries slaves were considered so absolutely the property of their owners, that they not only served themselves of them in the way of scortation and concubinage, but they were accustomed to accommodate their guests with them! Job is so conscious of his own innocence, that he is willing it should be put to the utmost proof; and if found guilty, that he may be exposed to the most distressing and humiliating punishment; even to that of being deprived of his goods, bereaved of his children, his wife made a slave, and subjected to all indignities in that state.
entries.108fe84feebae91d1483287f2728a9f9611f12c8: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen17429" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17430" type="x-p"/> For this is a heinous crime - Mr. Good translates, "For this would be a premeditated crime, <div eID="gen17430" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17431" type="x-p"/> And a profligacy of the understanding." <div eID="gen17431" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17432" type="x-p"/> See also <reference osisRef="Job.31.28">Job 31:28</reference>. That is, It would not only be a sin against the individuals more particularly concerned, but a sin of the first magnitude against society; and one of which the civil magistrate should take particular cognizance, and punish as justice requires.
entries.acb63c7fb70111e05605fa6d54c788c42ee76beb: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen17432" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17433" type="x-p"/> For it is a fire - Nothing is so destructive of domestic peace. Where jealousy exists, unmixed misery dwells; and the adulterer and fornicator waste their substance on the unlawful objects of their impure affections.
entries.1d52ccc9b4dc0fc2faa384da0708a4cfc4039da3: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen17433" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17434" type="x-p"/> The cause of my man-servant - In ancient times slaves had no action at law against their owners; they might dispose of them as they did of their cattle, or any other property. The slave might complain; and the owner might hear him if he pleased, but he was not compelled to do so. Job states that he had admitted them to all civil rights; and, far from preventing their case from being heard, he was ready to permit them to complain even against himself, if they had a cause of complaint, and to give them all the benefit of the law.
entries.8d2be0b0ee3df6878299c6578077345a53e53688: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen17434" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17435" type="x-p"/> Did not he that made me - make him? - I know that God is the Judge of all; that all shall appear before him in that state where the king and his subject, the master and his slave, shall be on an equal footing, all civil distinctions being abolished for ever. If, then I had treated my slaves with injustice, how could I stand before the judgment-seat of God? I have treated others as I wish to be treated.
entries.c0f9aea24ea7130fc59735c5faf16a6775da4b0d: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen17435" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17436" type="x-p"/> Or have eaten my morsel myself alone - Hospitality was a very prominent virtue among the ancients in almost all nations: friends and strangers were equally welcome to the board of the affluent. The supper was their grand meal: it was then that they saw their friends; the business and fatigues of the day being over, they could then enjoy themselves comfortably together. The supper was called coena on this account; or, as Plutarch says, Το μεν γαρ δειπνον φασι κοινα δια την κοινωνιαν καλεισθαι· καθ' ἑαυτους γαρ ηριστων επιεικως οἱ παλαι ρωμαιοι, συνδειπνουντες τοις φιλοις. "The ancient Romans named supper Coena, (κοινα), which signifies communion (κοινωνια) or fellowship; for although they dined alone, they supped with their friends." - Plut. Symp. lib. viii., prob. 6, p. 687. But Job speaks here of dividing his bread with the hungry: Or have eaten my morsel myself alone. And he is a poor despicable caitiff who would eat it alone, while there was another at hand, full as hungry as himself.
entries.a7e66c9580378f8f221828608ccf45f4cfe71e34: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen17436" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17437" type="x-p"/> This is a very difficult verse, and is variously translated. Take the following instances: - For from his youth he (the male orphan) was brought up with me as a father. Yea, I have guided her (the female orphan) from her mother's womb - Heath. <div eID="gen17437" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17438" type="x-p"/> Nam a pueris educavit me commiseratio; jam inde ab utero matris meae illa me deduxit - Houbigant. "For commiseration educated me from my childhood; <div eID="gen17438" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17439" type="x-p"/> And she brought me up even from my mother's womb." <div eID="gen17439" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17440" type="x-p"/> This is agreeable to the Vulgate. "Behold, from my youth calamity hath quickened me; <div eID="gen17440" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17441" type="x-p"/> Even from my mother's womb have I distributed it." <div eID="gen17441" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17442" type="x-p"/> This is Mr. Goods version, and is widely different from the above. <div eID="gen17442" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17443" type="x-p"/> For mercy grewe up with me fro my youth, <div eID="gen17443" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17444" type="x-p"/> And compassion fro my mother's wombe. <div eID="gen17444" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17445" type="x-p"/> Coverdale. Ὁτι εκ νεοτητος μου εξετρεφον ὡς πατηρ, και εκ γαστρος μητρος μου ὡδηγησα - Septuagint. "For from my youth I nourished them as a father; and I was their guide from my mother's womb." <div eID="gen17445" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17446" type="x-p"/> The Syriac. - "For from my childhood he educated me in distresses, and from the womb of my mother in groans." The Arabic is nearly the same. <div eID="gen17446" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17447" type="x-p"/> The general meaning may be gathered from the above; but who can reconcile such discordant translations?
entries.e21c20ba6592113031ad35be9b8b64a70a1cd018: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen17447" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17448" type="x-p"/> If his loins have not blessed me - This is a very delicate touch: the part that was cold and shivering is now covered with warm woollen. It feels the comfort; and by a fine prosopopoeia, is represented as blessing him who furnished the clothing.
entries.35247da256f803990dd75dd7582be8460eee43da: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen17448" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17449" type="x-p"/> If I have lifted up my hand against the fatherless - I have at no time opposed the orphan, nor given, in behalf of the rich and powerful, a decision against the poor, when I saw my help in the gate - when I was sitting chief on the throne of judgment, and could have done it without being called to account. There are sentiments very like these in the poem of Lebeid, one of the authors of the Moallakhat. I shall quote several verses from the elegant translation of Sir William Jones, in which the character of a charitable and bountiful chief is well described: - "Oft have I invited a numerous company to the death of a camel bought for slaughter, to be divided with arrows of equal dimensions." "I invite them to draw lots for a camel without a foal, and for a camel with her young one, whose flesh I distribute to all the neighbors." "The guest and the stranger admitted to my board seem to have alighted in the sweet vale of Tebaala, luxuriant with vernal blossoms." "The cords of my tent approaches every needy matron, worn with fatigue, like a camel doomed to die at her master's tomb, whose venture is both scanty and ragged." "There they crown with meat (while the wintry winds contend with fierce blasts) a dish flowing like a rivulet, into which the famished orphans eagerly plunge." "He distributes equal shares, he dispenses justice to the tribes, he is indignant when their right is diminished; and, to establish their right, often relinquishes his own." "He acts with greatness of mind, and nobleness of heart: he sheds the dew of his liberality on those who need his assistance; he scatters around his own gains and precious spoils, the prizes of his valor." - Ver. 73-80.
entries.89f6684a10c6939555b70d8801bcded4712303c7: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen17449" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17450" type="x-p"/> Let mine arm fall - Mr. Good, as a medical man, is at home in the translation of this verse: - "May my shoulder-bone be shivered at the blade, <div eID="gen17450" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17451" type="x-p"/> And mine arm be broken off at the socket." <div eID="gen17451" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17452" type="x-p"/> Let judgment fall particularly on those parts which have either done wrong, or refused to do right when in their power.
entries.301d84a8ff319ca5c697c5ee8b2e58388b373460: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen17452" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17453" type="x-p"/> Destruction from God was a terror - I have ever been preserved from outward sin, through the fear of God's judgments; I knew his eye was constantly upon me, and I could "Never in my Judge's eye my Judge's anger dare."
entries.1c3fc8125f96f9d28a740b0028ca4227347649ff: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen17453" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17454" type="x-p"/> Gold my hope - For the meaning of זהב zahab, polished gold, and כתם kethem, stamped gold, see on <reference osisRef="Job.28.15-Job.28.17">Job 28:15-17</reference> (note).
entries.1f25cf8994adbb6a3fec80ba5f0c15c3ff8091ee: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen17454" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17455" type="x-p"/> If I beheld the sun when it shined - In this verse Job clears himself of that idolatrous worship which was the most ancient and most consistent with reason of any species of idolatry; viz., Sabaeism, the worship of the heavenly bodies; particularly the sun and moon, Jupiter and Venus, the two latter being the morning and evening stars, and the most resplendent of all the heavenly bodies, the sun and moon excepted. "Job," says Calmet, "points out three things here: <div eID="gen17455" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17456" type="x-p"/> 1. The worship of the sun and moon; much used in his time, and very anciently used in every part of the East; and in all probability that from which idolatry took its rise. <div eID="gen17456" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17457" type="x-p"/> 2. The custom of adoring the sun at its rising, and the moon at her change; a superstition which is mentioned in <reference osisRef="Eze.8.16">Eze 8:16</reference>, and in every part of profane antiquity. <div eID="gen17457" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17458" type="x-p"/> 3. The custom of kissing the hand; the form of adoration, and token of sovereign respect."Adoration, or the religious act of kissing the hand, comes to us from the Latin; ad, to, and os, oris, the mouth. The hand lifted to the mouth, and there saluted by the lips.
entries.dd64495c3377d54af24f816cbb70454fa448c2aa: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen17458" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17459" type="x-p"/> For I should have denied the God that is above - Had I paid Divine adoration to them, I should have thereby denied the God that made them.
entries.d0933c01130a5fc730a744499b926a04f247e8fe: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen17459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17460" type="x-p"/> If I rejoiced - I did not avenge myself on my enemy; and I neither bore malice nor hatred to him.
entries.d7aa8522d1acb9591160d4c28dddef6170ea4a66: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen17460" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17461" type="x-p"/> Neither have I suffered my mouth to sin - I have neither spoken evil of him, nor wished evil to him. How few of those called Christians can speak thus concerning their enemies; or those who have done them any mischief!
entries.ff9085e6e76d6ec31d568ee80b3acb283b724560: <hi type="bold">Verse 31</hi> <div eID="gen17461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17462" type="x-p"/> If the men of my tabernacle said - I believe the Targum gives the best sense here: - "If the men of my tabernacle have not said, Who hath commanded that we should not be satisfied with his flesh?" My domestics have had all kindness shown them; they have lived like my own children, and have been served with the same viands as my family. They have never seen flesh come to my table, when they have been obliged to live on pulse. Mr. Good's translation is nearly to the same sense: - "If the men of my tabernacle do not exclaim, <div eID="gen17462" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17463" type="x-p"/> Who hath longed for his meat without fullness?" "Where is the man that has not been satisfied with his flesh?" i.e., fed to the full with the provisions from his table. See <reference osisRef="Pro.23.20">Pro 23:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.23.13">Isa 23:13</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Dan.10.3">Dan 10:3</reference>.
entries.0f8b07f0fcf18261e85851ae0191b450b3ed9a02: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen17463" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17464" type="x-p"/> The stranger did not lodge in the street - My kindness did not extend merely to my family, domestics, and friends; the stranger - he who was to me perfectly unknown, and the traveler - he who was on his journey to some other district, found my doors ever open to receive them, and were refreshed with my bed and my board.
entries.ef6c246f16da9472cc9abcd781b96613efb051cd: <hi type="bold">Verse 33</hi> <div eID="gen17464" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17465" type="x-p"/> If I covered my transgressions as Adam - Here is a most evident allusion to the fall. Adam transgressed the commandment of his Maker, and he endeavored to conceal it; first, by hiding himself among the trees of the garden: "I heard thy voice, and went and Hid myself;" secondly, by laying the blame on his wife: "The woman gave me, and I did eat;" and thirdly, by charging the whole directly on God himself: "The woman which Thou Gavest Me to be with me, She gave me of the tree, and I did eat." And it is very likely that Job refers immediately to the Mosaic account in the Book of Genesis. The spirit of this saying is this: When I have departed at any time from the path of rectitude, I have been ready to acknowledge my error, and have not sought excuses or palliatives for my sin.
entries.e675915a4f28be7a95e0a1e0cbe70f3263b5d1cd: <hi type="bold">Verse 34</hi> <div eID="gen17465" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17466" type="x-p"/> Did I fear a great multitude - Was I ever prevented by the voice of the many from decreeing and executing what was right? When many families or tribes espoused a particular cause, which I found, on examination, to be wrong, did they put me in fear, so as to prevent me from doing justice to the weak and friendless? Or, in any of these cases, was I ever, through fear, self-seeking, or favor, prevented from declaring my mind, or constrained to keep my house, lest I should be obliged to give judgment against my conscience? Mr. Good thinks it an imprecation upon himself, if he had done any of the evils which he mentions in the preceding verse. He translates thus: - "Then let me be confounded before the assembled multitude, <div eID="gen17466" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17467" type="x-p"/> And let the reproach of its families quash me! <div eID="gen17467" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17468" type="x-p"/> Yea, let me be struck dumb! let me never appear abroad!" <div eID="gen17468" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17469" type="x-p"/> I am satisfied that <reference osisRef="Job.31.38-Job.31.40">Job 31:38-40</reference>, should come in either here, or immediately after <reference osisRef="Job.31.25">Job 31:25</reference>; and that Job's words should end with <reference osisRef="Job.31.37">Job 31:37</reference>, which, if the others were inserted in their proper places, would be <reference osisRef="Job.31.40">Job 31:40</reference>. See the reasons at the end of the chapter, <reference osisRef="Job.31.40">Job 31:40</reference> (note).
entries.07d9d66b11f3a6dad587115920ccbe8b00787e65: <hi type="bold">Verse 35</hi> <div eID="gen17469" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17470" type="x-p"/> O that one would hear me! - I wish to have a fair and full hearing: I am grievously accused; and have no proper opportunity of clearing myself, and establishing my own innocence. <div eID="gen17470" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17471" type="x-p"/> Behold, my desire is - Or, הן תוי hen tavi, "There is my pledge." I bind myself, on a great penalty, to come into court, and abide the issue. <div eID="gen17471" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17472" type="x-p"/> That the Almighty would answer me - That he would call this case immediately before himself; and oblige my adversary to come into court, to put his accusations into a legal form, that I might have the opportunity of vindicating myself in the presence of a judge who would hear dispassionately my pleadings, and bring the cause to a righteous issue. <div eID="gen17472" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17473" type="x-p"/> And that mine adversary had written a book - That he would not indulge himself in vague accusations, but would draw up a proper bill of indictment, that I might know to what I had to plead, and find the accusation in a tangible form.
entries.abdbd0f8ad369ebd940fd092a68dee8c2c572325: <hi type="bold">Verse 36</hi> <div eID="gen17473" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17474" type="x-p"/> Surely I would take it upon my shoulder - I would be contented to stand before the bar as a criminal, bearing upon my shoulder the board to which the accusation is affixed. In a book of Chinese punishments now before me, containing drawings representing various criminals brought to trial, in trial, and after trial, charged with different offenses; in almost all of them a board appears, on which the accusation or crime of which they are accused, or for which they suffer, is fairly written. Where the punishment is capital, this board appears fastened to the instrument, or stuck near the place of punishment. In one case a large, heavy plank, through which there is a hole to pass the head, - or rather a hole fitting the neck, like that in the pillory, - with the crime written upon it, rests on the criminal's shoulders; and this he is obliged to carry about for the weeks or months during which the punishment lasts. It is probable that Job alludes to something of this kind, which he intimates he would bear about with him during the interim between accusation and the issue in judgment; and, far from considering this a disgrace, would clasp it as dearly as he would adjust a crown or diadem to his head; being fully assured, from his innocence, and the evidence of it, which would infallibly appear on the trial, that he would have the most honorable acquittal. There may also be an allusion to the manner of receiving a favor from a superior: it is immediately placed on the head, as a mark of respect; and if a piece of cloth be given at the temple, the receiver not only puts it on his head, but binds it there.
entries.86fec9e968548633714644b7a1992ac3ce270769: <hi type="bold">Verse 37</hi> <div eID="gen17474" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17475" type="x-p"/> I would declare unto him the number of my steps - I would show this adversary the different stations I had been in, and the offices which I had filled in life, that he might trace me through the whole of my civil, military, and domestic life, in order to get evidence against me. <div eID="gen17475" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17476" type="x-p"/> As a prince would I go near - Though carrying my own accusation, I would go into the presence of my judge as the נגיד nagid, chief, or sovereign commander and judge, of the people and country, and would not shrink from having my conduct investigated by even the meanest of my subjects. In these three verses we may observe the following particulars: - <div eID="gen17476" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17477" type="x-p"/> 1. Job wishes to be brought to trial, that he might have the opportunity of vindicating himself: O that I might have a hearing! <div eID="gen17477" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17478" type="x-p"/> 2. That his adversary, Eliphaz and his companions, whom he considers as one party, and joined together in one, would reduce their vague charges to writing, that they might come before the court in a legal form: O that my adversary would write down the charge! <div eID="gen17478" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17479" type="x-p"/> 3. That the Almighty, שדי Shaddai, the all-sufficient God, and not man, should be the judge, who would not permit his adversaries to attempt, by false evidence, to establish what was false, nor suffer himself to cloak with a hypocritical covering what was iniquitous in his conduct: O that the Almighty might answer for me - take notice of or be judge in the cause! <div eID="gen17479" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17480" type="x-p"/> 4. To him he purposes cheerfully to confess all his ways, who could at once judge if he prevaricated, or concealed the truth. <div eID="gen17480" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17481" type="x-p"/> 5. This would give him the strongest encouragement: he would go boldly before him, with the highest persuasion of an honorable acquittal.
entries.99301f589b5ba222200e8c79626357c22621ef78: <hi type="bold">Verse 38</hi> <div eID="gen17481" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17482" type="x-p"/> If my land cry - The most careless reader may see that the introduction of this and the two following verses here, disturbs the connection, and that they are most evidently out of their place. Job seems here to refer to that law, <reference osisRef="Lev.25.1-Lev.25.7">Lev 25:1-7</reference>, by which the Israelites were obliged to give the land rest every seventh year, that the soil might not be too much exhausted by perpetual cultivation, especially in a country which afforded so few advantages to improve the arable ground by manure. He, conscious that he had acted according to this law, states that his land could not cry out against him, nor its furrows complain. He had not broken the law, nor exhausted the soil.
entries.951690afa2701d94ab37d2fb1da24089da3f0555: <hi type="bold">Verse 39</hi> <div eID="gen17482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17483" type="x-p"/> If I have eaten the fruits thereof without money - I have never been that narrow-minded man who, through a principle of covetousness, exhausts his land, putting himself to no charges, by labor and manure, to strengthen it; or defrauds those of their wages who were employed under him. If I have eaten the fruits of it, I have cultivated it well to produce those fruits; and this has not been without money, for I have gone to expenses on the soil, and remunerated the laborers. <div eID="gen17483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17484" type="x-p"/> Or have caused the owners thereof to lose their life - Coverdale translates, Yee yf I have greved eny of the plowmen. They have not panted in labor without due recompense.
entries.af9adb09f59cace6bae7e45196c6aa05bc5c3ff4: <hi type="bold">Verse 40</hi> <div eID="gen17484" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17485" type="x-p"/> Let thistles grow instead of wheat - What the word חוח choach means, which we translate thistles, we cannot tell: but as חח chach seems to mean to hold, catch as a hook, to hitch, it must signify some kind of hooked thorn, like the brier; and this is possibly its meaning. <div eID="gen17485" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17486" type="x-p"/> And cockle - באשה bashah, some fetid plant, from באש baash, to stink. In <reference osisRef="Isa.5.2">Isa 5:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.5.4">Isa 5:4</reference>, we translate it wild grapes; and Bishop Lowth, poisonous berries: but Hasselquist, a pupil of the famous Linnaeus, in his Voyages, p. 289, is inclined to believe that the solanum incanum, or hoary nightshade is meant, as this is common in Egypt, Palestine, and the East. Others are of opinion that it means the aconite, which (Arabic) beesh, in Arabic, denotes: this is a poisonous herb, and grows luxuriantly on the sunny hills among the vineyards, according to Celsus in Hieroboticon. (Arabic) beesh is not only the name of an Indian poisonous herb, called the napellus moysis, but (Arabic) beesh moosh, or (Arabic) farut al beesh, is the name of an animal, resembling a mouse, which lives among the roots of this very plant. "May I have a crop of this instead of barley, if I have acted improperly either by my land or my laborers!" <div eID="gen17486" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17487" type="x-p"/> The words of Job are ended - That is, his defense of himself against the accusations of his friends, as they are called. He spoke afterwards, but never to them; he only addresses God, who came to determine the whole controversy. These words seem very much like an addition by a later hand. They are wanting in many of the MSS. of the Vulgate, two in my own possession; and in the Editio Princeps of this version. I suppose that at first they were inserted in rubric, by some scribe, and afterwards taken into the text. In a MS. of my own, of the twelfth or thirteenth century, these words stand in rubric, actually detached from the text; while in another MS., of the fourteenth century, they form a part of the text. In the Hebrew text they are also detached: the hemistichs are complete without them; nor indeed can they be incorporated with them. They appear to me an addition of no authority. In the first edition of our Bible, that by Coverdale, 1535, there is a white line between these words and the conclusion of the chapter; and they stand, forming no part of the text, thus: <div eID="gen17487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17488" type="x-p"/> Here ende the wordes of Job. <div eID="gen17488" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17489" type="x-p"/> Just as we say, in reading the Scriptures "Here ends such a chapter;" or, "Here ends the first lesson," etc. Or the subject of the transposition, mentioned above, I have referred to the reasons at the end of the chapter. Dr. Kennicott, on this subject, observes: "Chapters 29, 30, and 31, contain Job's animated self-defense, which was made necessary by the reiterated accusation of his friends. This defense now concludes with six lines (in the Hebrew text) which declare, that if he had enjoyed his estates covetously, or procured them unjustly, he wished them to prove barren and unprofitable. This part, therefore seems naturally to follow <reference osisRef="Job.31.25">Job 31:25</reference>, where he speaks of his gold, and how much his hand had gotten. The remainder of the chapter will then consist of these four regular parts, viz., <div eID="gen17489" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17490" type="x-p"/> 1. His piety to God, in his freedom from idolatry, <reference osisRef="Job.31.26-Job.31.28">Job 31:26-28</reference>. <div eID="gen17490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17491" type="x-p"/> 2. His benevolence to men, in his charity both of temper and behavior, <reference osisRef="Job.31.29-Job.31.32">Job 31:29-32</reference>. <div eID="gen17491" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17492" type="x-p"/> 3. His solemn assurance that he did not conceal his guilt, from fearing either the violence of the poor, or the contempt of the rich, <reference osisRef="Job.31.33">Job 31:33</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.31.34">Job 31:34</reference>. <div eID="gen17492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17493" type="x-p"/> 4. (Which must have been the last article, because conclusive of the work) he infers that, being thus secured by his integrity, he may appeal safely to God himself. This appeal he therefore makes boldly, and in such words as, when rightly translated, form an image which perhaps has no parallel. For where is there an image so magnificent or so splendid as this? <div eID="gen17493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17494" type="x-p"/> Job, thus conscious of innocence, wishing even God himself to draw up his indictment, [rather his adversary Eliphaz and companions to draw up this indictment, the Almighty to be judge,] that very indictment he would bind round his head; and with that indictment as his crown of glory, he would, with the dignity of a prince, advance to his trial! Of this wonderful passage I add a version more just and more intelligible than the present: - " <div eID="gen17494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17495" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 35</hi> <div eID="gen17495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17496" type="x-p"/> O that one would grant me a hearing! <div eID="gen17496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17497" type="x-p"/> Behold, my desire is that the Almighty would answer me; <div eID="gen17497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17498" type="x-p"/> And, as plaintiff against me, draw up the indictment. <div eID="gen17498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17499" type="x-p"/> With what earnestness would I take it on my shoulders! <div eID="gen17499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17500" type="x-p"/> I would bind it upon me as a diadem. <div eID="gen17500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17501" type="x-p"/> The number of my steps would I set forth unto Him; <div eID="gen17501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17502" type="x-p"/> Even as a prince would I approach before Him!" <div eID="gen17502" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17503" type="x-p"/> I have already shown that Eliphaz and his companions, not God, are the adversary or plaintiff of whom Job speaks. This view makes the whole clear and consistent, and saves Job from the charge of presumptuous rashness. See also Kennicott's Remarks, p. 163. It would not be right to say that no other interpretation has been given of the first clause of <reference osisRef="Job.31.10">Job 31:10</reference> than that given above. The manner in which Coverdale has translated the <reference osisRef="Job.31.9">Job 31:9</reference> and <reference osisRef="Job.31.10">Job 31:10</reference> is the way in which they are generally understood: Yf my hert hath lusted after my neghbour's wife, or yf I have layed wayte at his dore; O then let my wife be another man's harlot, and let other lye with her. <div eID="gen17503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17504" type="x-p"/> In this sense the word grind is not unfrequently used by the ancients. Horace represents the divine Cato commending the young men whom he saw frequenting the stews, because they left other men's wives undefiled! <div eID="gen17504" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17505" type="x-p"/> Virtute esto, inquit sententia dia Catonis, <div eID="gen17505" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17506" type="x-p"/> Nam simul ac venas inflavit tetra libido, <div eID="gen17506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17507" type="x-p"/> Hue juvenes aequum est descendere, non alienas <div eID="gen17507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17508" type="x-p"/> Permolere uxores. <div eID="gen17508" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17509" type="x-p"/> Sat. lib. i., s. 2, ver. 32. "When awful Cato saw a noted spark <div eID="gen17509" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17510" type="x-p"/> From a night cellar stealing in the dark: 'Well done, my friend, if lust thy heart inflame, <div eID="gen17510" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17511" type="x-p"/> Indulge it here, and spare the married dame.'" <div eID="gen17511" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17512" type="x-p"/> Francis. <div eID="gen17512" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17513" type="x-p"/> Such were the morals of the holiest state of heathen Rome; and even of Cato, the purest and severest censor of the public manners! O tempora! O mores! I may add from a scholiast: - Molere vetus verbum est pro adulterare, subagitare, quo verbo in deponenti significatione utitur alibi Ausonius, inquiens, Epigr. vii., ver. 6, de crispa impudica et detestabili: - <div eID="gen17513" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17514" type="x-p"/> Deglubit, fellat, molitur, per utramque cavernam. <div eID="gen17514" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17515" type="x-p"/> Qui enim coit, quasi molere et terere videtur. <div eID="gen17515" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17516" type="x-p"/> Hinc etiam molitores dicti sunt, subactores, ut apud eundem, Epigr. xc., ver. 3. <div eID="gen17516" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17517" type="x-p"/> Cum dabit uxori molitor tuus, et tibi adulter. <div eID="gen17517" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17518" type="x-p"/> Thus the rabbins understand what is spoken of Samson grinding in the prison-house: quod ad ipsum Palaestini certatim suas uxores adduxerunt, suscipiendae ex eo prolis causa, ob ipsius robur. In this sense St. Jerome understands <reference osisRef="Lam.5.13">Lam 5:13</reference> : They took the young men to Grind. Adolescentibus ad impudicitiam sunt abusi, ad concubitum scilicet nefandum. Concerning grinding of corn, by portable millstones, or querns, and that this was the work of females alone, and they the meanest slaves; see the note on <reference osisRef="Exo.11.5">Exo 11:5</reference>, and on <reference osisRef="Jdg.16.21">Jdg 16:21</reference>. The Greeks use μυλλας to signify a harlot; and μυλλω, to grind, and also coeo, ineo, in the same sense in which Horace, as quoted above, alienas Permolere uxores. So Theocritus, Idyll. iv., ver. 58. Ειπ' αγε μοι Κορυδων, το γεροντιον η ῥ' ετι μυλλει Τηναν ταν κυανοφρυν ερωτιδα, τας ποτ' εκνισθη· <div eID="gen17518" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17519" type="x-p"/> Dic age mihi, Corydon, senecio ille num adhuc molit, <div eID="gen17519" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17520" type="x-p"/> Illud nigro supercilio scortillum, quod olim deperibat? <div eID="gen17520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17521" type="x-p"/> Hence the Greek paronomasia, μυλλαδα μυλλειν, scortam molere. I need make no apology for leaving the principal part of this note in a foreign tongue. To those for whom it is designed it will be sufficiently plain. If the above were Job's meaning, how dreadful is the wish or imprecation in verse the tenth!  <chapter eID="Job.31"/> <div eID="gen17521" type="x-p"/>

entries.793bd6338141de928a3219348fc9bec54d5e4e38: <reference osisRef="Job.31.1-Job.4.1">Job 31:1-4   1</reference>  I have made a covenant with mine eyes, <div eID="gen8238" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8239" type="x-p"/> And how should I fix my gaze upon a maiden!   2  What then would be the dispensation of Eloah from above, <div eID="gen8239" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8240" type="x-p"/> And the inheritance of the Almighty from the heights -   3  Doth not calamity overtake the wicked, <div eID="gen8240" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8241" type="x-p"/> And misfortune the workers of evil?   4  Doth He not see my ways <div eID="gen8241" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8242" type="x-p"/> And count all my steps? <div eID="gen8242" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8243" type="x-p"/> After Job has described and bewailed the harsh contrast between the former days and the present, he gives us a picture of his moral life and endeavour, in connection with the character of which the explanation of his present affliction as a divinely decreed punishment becomes impossible, and the sudden overthrow of his prosperity into this abyss of suffering becomes to him, for the same reason, the most painful mystery. Job is not an Israelite, he is without the pale of the positive, Sinaitic revelation; his religion is the old patriarchal religion, which even in the present day is called <hi type="italic">dı̂n Ibrâhı̂m</hi> (the religion of Abraham), or <hi type="italic">dı̂n el - bedu</hi> (the religion of the steppe) as the religion of those Arabs who are not Moslem, or at least influenced by the penetrating Islamism, and is called by Mejânı̂shı̂ <hi type="italic">el - hanı̂fı̂je</hi> (vid., <hi type="italic">supra</hi>, p. 362, note) as the patriarchally orthodox religion.<note placement="foot">Also in the <hi type="italic">Merg</hi> district east of Damascus, which is peopled by an ancient unmixed race, because the fever which prevails there kills strangers, remnants of the <hi type="italic">dı̂n Ibrâhı̂m</hi> have been preserved despite the penetrating Islamism. There the <hi type="italic">mulaqqin</hi> (Souffleur), who says the creed into the grave as a farewell to the buried one, adds the following words: “The <hi type="italic">muslim</hi> is my brother, the <hi type="italic">muslima</hi> my sister, Abraham is my father (<hi type="italic">abı̂</hi>), his religion (<hi type="italic">dı̂nuh</hi>) is mine, and his confession (<hi type="italic">medhebuh</hi>) mine.” It is indisputable that the words <hi type="italic">muslim</hi> (one who is submissive to God) and <hi type="italic">islâm</hi> (submission to God) have originally belonged to the <hi type="italic">dı̂n Ibrâhı̂m</hi>. It is also remarkable that the Moslem salutation <hi type="italic">selâm</hi> occurs only as a sign in war among the wandering tribes, and that the guest parts from his host with the words: <hi type="italic">dâimâ besât el - Chalı̂l̂ lâ maqtû‛ walâ memnû‛ ,</hi> i.e., mayest thou always have Abraham’s table, and plenty of provisions and guests. - Wetzst.</note> <div eID="gen8243" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8244" type="x-p"/> As little as this religion, even in the present day, is acquainted with the specific Mohammedan commandments, so little knew Job of the specifically Israelitish. On the contrary, his confession, which he lays down in this third monologue, coincides remarkably with the ten commandments of piety (<hi type="italic">el - felâh</hi>) peculiar to the <hi type="italic">dı̂n Ibrâhı̂m</hi>, although it differs in this respect, that it does not give the prominence to submission to the dispensations of God, that <hi type="italic">teslı̂m</hi> which, as the whole of this didactic poem teaches by its issue, is the duty of the perfectly pious; also bravery in defence of holy property and rights is wanting, which among the wandering tribes is accounted as an essential part of the <hi type="italic">hebbet er - rı̂h</hi> (inspiration of the Divine Being), i.e., active piety, and to which it is similarly related, as to the binding notion of “honour” which was coined by the western chivalry of the middle ages. <div eID="gen8244" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8245" type="x-p"/> Job begins with the duty of chastity. Consistently with the prologue, which the drama itself nowhere belies, he is living in monogamy, as at the present day the orthodox Arabs, averse to Islamism, are not addicted to Moslem polygamy. With the confession of having maintained this marriage (although, to infer from the prologue, it was not an over-happy, deeply sympathetic one) sacred, and restrained himself not only from every adulterous act, but also from adulterous desires, his confessions begin. Here, in the middle of the Old Testament, without the pale of the Old Testament νόμος, we meet just that moral strictness and depth with which the Preacher on the mount, Mat 5:27., opposes the spirit to the letter of the seventh commandment. It is לעיני, not עם־עיני, designedly; כרת ברית עם or את is the usual phrase where two equals are concerned; on the contrary, כרת ברית ל where two the superior - Jehovah, or a king, or conqueror - binds himself to another under prescribed conditions, or the covenant is made not so much by a mutual advance as by the one taking the initiative. In this latter case, the secondary notions of a promise given (e.g., <reference osisRef="Isa.55.3">Isa 55:3</reference>), or even, as here, of a law prescribed, are combined with כרת ברית: “as lord of my senses I prescribed this law for my eyes” (Ew.). The eyes, says a Talmudic proverb, are the procuresses of sin (סרסורי דחטאה נינהו); “to close his eyes, that they may not feast on evil,” is, in <reference osisRef="Isa.33.15">Isa 33:15</reference>, a clearly defined line in the picture of him on whom the everlasting burnings can have no hold. The exclamation, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.31.1">Job 31:1</reference></hi>, is spoken with self-conscious indignation: Why should I... (comp. Joseph’s exclamation, <reference osisRef="Gen.39.9">Gen 39:9</reference>); Schultens correctly: <hi type="italic">est indignatio repellens vehementissime et negans tale quicquam committi par esse;</hi> the transition of the מה, Arab. <hi type="italic">mâ</hi>, to the expression of negation, which is complete in Arabic, is here in its incipient state, Ew. §325, <hi type="italic">b</hi>. התבּונן על is intended to express a fixed and inspection (comp. אל, 1Ki 3:21) gaze upon an object, combined with a lascivious imagination (comp. Sir. 9:5, παρθένον μὴ καταμάνθανε, and 9:8, ἀπόστρεψον ὀφθαλμὸν ἀπὸ γυναικὸς εὐμόρφου καὶ μὴ καταμάνθανε κάλλος ἀλλότριον), a βλέπειν which issues in ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτῆν, Mat 5:28. <hi type="italic">Adulterium reale,</hi> and in fact two-sided, is first spoken of in the third strophe, here it is <hi type="italic">adulterium mentale</hi> and one-sided; the object named is not any maiden whatever, but any בּתוּלה, because virginity is ever to be revered, a most sacred thing, the holy purity of which Job acknowledges himself to have guarded against profanation from any lascivious gaze by keeping a strict watch over his eyes. The <hi type="italic">Waw</hi> of וּמה is, as in <reference osisRef="Job.31.14">Job 31:14</reference>, copulative: and if I had done it, what punishment might I have looked for? <div eID="gen8245" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8246" type="x-p"/> The question, <reference osisRef="Job.31.2">Job 31:2</reference>, is proposed in order that it may be answered in <reference osisRef="Job.31.3">Job 31:3</reference> again in the form of a question: in consideration of the just punishment which the injurer of female innocence meets, Job disavows every unchaste look. On חלק and נחלה used of allotted, adjudged punishment, comp. <reference osisRef="Job.20.29">Job 20:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.27.13">Job 27:13</reference>; on נכר, which alternates with איד (burden of suffering, misfortune), comp. Oba 1:12, where in its stead נכר occurs, as Arab. <hi type="italic">nukr</hi>, properly <hi type="italic">id quod patienti paradoxum, insuetum, intolerabile videtur, omne ingratum</hi> (Reiske). Conscious of the just punishment of the unchaste, and, as he adds in <reference osisRef="Job.31.4">Job 31:4</reference>, of the omniscience of the heavenly Judge, Job has made dominion over sin, even in its first beginnings and motions, his principle. <div eID="gen8246" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8247" type="x-p"/> The הוּא, which gives prominence to the subject, means Him who punishes the unchaste. By Him who observes his walk on every side, and counts (יספּור, <hi type="italic">plene</hi>, according to Ew. §138, <hi type="italic">a</hi>, on account of the pause, but vid., the similar form of writing, <reference osisRef="Job.39.2">Job 39:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.18.15">Job 18:15</reference>) all his steps, Job has been kept back from sin, and to Him Job can appeal as a witness.
entries.0aa16a375bb2a1dc6d1a872eb8b33927563e1b51: <reference osisRef="Job.31.5-Job.8.5">Job 31:5-8   5</reference>  If I had intercourse with falsehood, <div eID="gen8247" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8248" type="x-p"/> And my foot hastened after deceit:   6  Let Him weigh me in the balances of justice, <div eID="gen8248" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8249" type="x-p"/> And let Eloah know my innocence.   7  If my steps turned aside from the way, <div eID="gen8249" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8250" type="x-p"/> And my heart followed mine eyes, <div eID="gen8250" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8251" type="x-p"/> And any spot hath cleaved to my hands:   8  May I sow and another eat, <div eID="gen8251" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8252" type="x-p"/> And let my shoots be rooted out. <div eID="gen8252" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8253" type="x-p"/> We have translated שׁוא (on the form vid., on <reference osisRef="Job.15.31">Job 15:31</reference>, and the idea on <reference osisRef="Job.11.11">Job 11:11</reference>) falsehood, for it signifies desolateness and hollowness under a concealing mask, therefore the contradiction between what is without and within, lying and deceit, parall. מרמה, deceit, delusion, imposition. The phrase הלך עם־שׁוא is based on the personification of deceit, or on thinking of it in connection with the מתי־שׁוא (<reference osisRef="Job.11.11">Job 11:11</reference>). The form ותּחשׁ cannot be derived from חוּשׁ, from which it ought to be ותּחשׁ, like ויּסר Jdg 4:18 and freq., ויּשׂר (<hi type="italic">serravit</hi>) <reference osisRef="1Chr.20.3">1Ch 20:3</reference>, ויּעט (<hi type="italic">increpavit</hi>) 1Sa 25:14. Many grammarians (Ges. §72, rem. 9; Olsh. 257, g) explain the <hi type="italic">Pathach</hi> instead of <hi type="italic">Kametz</hi> as arising from the virtual doubling of the guttural (<hi type="italic">Dagesh forte implicitum</hi>), for which, however, no ground exists here; Ewald (§232, <hi type="italic">b</hi>) explains it by “the hastening of the tone towards the beginning,” which explains nothing, since the retreat of the tone has not this effect anywhere else. We must content ourselves with the supposition that ותּחשׁ is formed from a חשׁה having a similar meaning to חוּשׁ (חישׁ), as also ויּעט,   <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.19">1Sa 15:19</reference>, comp. <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.32">1Sa 14:32</reference>, is from a עטח of similar signification with עיט. The hypothetical antecedent, <reference osisRef="Job.31.5">Job 31:5</reference>, is followed by the conclusion, <reference osisRef="Job.31.6">Job 31:6</reference> : If he have done this, may God not spare him. He has, however, not done it; and if God puts him to an impartial trial, He will learn his תּמּה, <hi type="italic">integritas</hi>, purity of character. The “balance of justice” is the balance of the final judgment, which the Arabs call Arab. <hi type="italic">mı̂zân 'l - a‛mâl ,</hi> “the balance of actions (works).”<note placement="foot">The manual of ethics by Ghazzâli is entitled <hi type="italic">mı̂zân el - a‛mâl</hi> in the original, מאזני צדק in Bar-Chisdai’s translation, vid., Gosche on Ghazzâli’s life and works, S. 261 of the volume of the <hi type="italic">Berliner Akademie d. Wissensch.</hi> for 1858.</note> <div eID="gen8253" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8254" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Job.31.7">Job 31:7</reference> also begins hypothetically: if my steps (אשּׁוּרי from אשּׁוּר, which is used alternately with אשׁוּר without distinction, contrary to Ew. §260, <hi type="italic">b</hi>) swerve (תּטּה, the predicate to the <hi type="italic">plur</hi>. which follows, designating a thing, according to Ges. §146, 3) from the way (i.e., the one right way), and my heart went after my eyes, i.e., if it followed the drawing of the lust of the eye, viz., to obtain by deceit or extortion the property of another, and if a spot (מאוּם, <hi type="italic">macula</hi>, as <reference osisRef="Dan.1.4">Dan 1:4</reference>, = מוּם, <reference osisRef="Job.11.15">Job 11:15</reference>; according to Ew., equivalent to מחוּם, what is blackened and blackens, then a blemish, and according to Olsh., in מאוּמה...לא, like the French <hi type="italic">ne ... point</hi>) clave to my hands: I will sow, and let another eat, and let my shoots be rooted out. The poet uses צאצאים elsewhere of offspring of the body or posterity, <reference osisRef="Job.5.25">Job 5:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.21.8">Job 21:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.27.14">Job 27:14</reference>; here, however, as in Isaiah, with whom he has this word in common, <reference osisRef="Job.34.2">Job 34:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.42.5">Job 42:5</reference>, the produce of the ground is meant. <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.31.8">Job 31:8</reference></hi> is, according to Joh 4:37, a λόγος, a proverb. In so far as he may have acted thus, Job calls down upon himself the curse of Deut. 38:20f.: what he sows, let strangers reap and eat; and even when that which is sown does not fall into the hands of strangers, let it be uprooted.
entries.c4f7a96c1f33776621a7b74e566393ad62d83fe9: <reference osisRef="Job.31.9-Job.12.9">Job 31:9-12   9</reference>  If my heart has been befooled about a woman, <div eID="gen8254" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8255" type="x-p"/> And if I lay in wait at my neighbour’s door: 10  Let my wife grind unto another, <div eID="gen8255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8256" type="x-p"/> And let others bow down over her. 11  For this is an infamous act, <div eID="gen8256" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8257" type="x-p"/> And this is a crime to be brought before judges; 12  Yea, it is a fire that consumeth to the abyss, <div eID="gen8257" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8258" type="x-p"/> And should root out all my increase. <div eID="gen8258" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8259" type="x-p"/> As he has guarded himself against defiling virgin innocence by lascivious glances, so is he also conscious of having made no attempt to trespass upon the marriage relationship of his neighbour (רע as in the Decalogue, <reference osisRef="Exod.20.17">Exo 20:17</reference>): his heart was not persuaded, or he did not allow his heart to be persuaded (נפתּה like πείθεσθαι), i.e., misled, on account of a woman (אשּׁה as אשׁת אישׁ, in post-bibl. usage, of another’s wife), and he lay not in wait (according to the manner of adulterous lovers described at <reference osisRef="Job.24.15">Job 24:15</reference>, which see) at his neighbour’s door. We may here, with Wetzstein, compare the like-minded confession in a poem of Muhâdi ibn-Muhammel: Arab. <hi type="italic">mâ nabb klb 'l - jâr mnâ ẇlâ ‛awâ ,</hi> i.e., “The neighbour’s dog never barked (נב, Beduin equivalent to נבח in the Syrian towns and villages) on our account (because we have gone by night with an evil design to his tent), and it never howled (being beaten by us, to make it cease its barking lest it should betray us).” In <reference osisRef="Job.31.10">Job 31:10</reference> follows the punishment which he wishes might overtake him in case he had acted thus: “may my wife grind to another,” i.e., may she become his “maid behind the mill,” <reference osisRef="Exod.11.5">Exo 11:5</reference>, comp. <reference osisRef="Isa.47.2">Isa 47:2</reference>, who must allow herself to be used for everything; ἀλετρίς and a common low woman (comp. Plutarch, <hi type="italic">non posse suav.</hi> viv. c. 21, καὶ παχυσκελὴς ἀλετρὶς πρὸς μύλην κινουμένη) are almost one and the same. On the other hand, the Targ. (<hi type="italic">coeat cum alio</hi>), lxx (euphemistically ἀρέσαι ἑτέρῳ, not, as the Syr. Hexapl. shows, ἀλέσαι), and Jer. (<hi type="italic">scortum sit alterius</hi>), and in like manner Saad., Gecat., understand תּטחן directly of carnal surrender; and, in fact, according to the traditional opinion, <hi type="italic">b. Sota</hi> 10 <hi type="italic">a</hi>: אין טחינה אלא לשׁון עבירה, i.e., “טחן everywhere in Scripture is intended of (carnal) trespass.” With reference to Jdg 16:21 and <reference osisRef="Lam.5.13">Lam 5:13</reference> (where טחון, like Arab. <hi type="italic">ṭaḥûn</hi>, signifies the upper mill-stone, or in gen. the mill), this is certainly incorrect; the parallel, as well as <reference osisRef="Deut.28.30">Deu 28:30</reference>, favours this rendering of the word in the obscene sense of μύλλειν, <hi type="italic">molere</hi>, in this passage, which also is seen under the Arab. synon. of grinding, Arab. <hi type="italic">dahaka</hi> (<hi type="italic">trudere</hi>); according to which it would have to be interpreted: let her grind to another, i.e., serve him as it were as a nether mill-stone. The verb טחן, used elsewhere (in Talmud.) of the man, would here be transferred to the woman, like as it is used of the mill itself as that which grinds. This rendering is therefore not refuted by its being תּטחן and not תּטּחן. Moreover, the word thus understood is not unworthy of the poet, since he designedly makes Job seize the strongest expressions. Among moderns, תטחן is thus tropically explained by Ew., Umbr., Hahn, and a few others, but most expositors prefer the proper sense, in connection with which <hi type="italic">molat</hi> certainly, especially with respect to <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.31.9">Job 31:9</reference></hi>, is also equivalent to <hi type="italic">fiat pellex</hi>. It is hard to decide; nevertheless the preponderance of reasons seems to us to be on the side of the traditional tropical rendering, by the side of which <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.31.10">Job 31:10</reference></hi> is not attached in progressive, but in synonymous parallelism: <hi type="italic">et super ea incurvent se alii</hi>, כּרע of the man, as in the phrase Arab. <hi type="italic">kr‛t 'l - mrât 'lâ 'l - rjl</hi>(<hi type="italic">curvat se mulier ad virum</hi>) of the acquiescence of the woman; אחרין is a poetical Aramaism, Ew. §177, <hi type="italic">a</hi>. The sin of adultery, in case he had committed it, ought to be punished by another taking possession of his own wife, for that (הוּא a neutral <hi type="italic">masc., Keri</hi> היא in accordance with the <hi type="italic">fem</hi>. of the following predicate, comp. <reference osisRef="Lev.18.17">Lev 18:17</reference>) is an infamous act, and that (היא referring back to זמּה, <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> הוּא in accordance with the <hi type="italic">masc</hi>. of the following predicate) is a crime for the judges. On this wavering between הוא and היא vid., Gesenius, <hi type="italic">Handwörterbuch</hi>, 1863, <hi type="italic">s. v.</hi> הוּא, S. 225. זמּה is the usual Thora-word for the shameless subtle encroachments of sensual desires (vid., Saalschütz, <hi type="italic">Mosaisches Recht,</hi> S. 791f.), and פּלילים עון (not עון), according to the usual view equivalent to <hi type="italic">crimen et crimen quidem judicum</hi> (however, on the form of connection intentionally avoided here, where the genitival relation might easily give an erroneous sense, vid., Ges. §116, rem.), signifies a crime which falls within the province of the penal code, for which in <reference osisRef="Job.31.28">Job 31:28</reference> it is less harshly עון פּלילי: a judicial, i.e., criminal offence. פּלילים is, moreover, not the <hi type="italic">plur</hi>. of פּלילי (Kimchi), but of פּליל, an arbitrator (root פל, <hi type="italic">findere, dirimere</hi>). <div eID="gen8259" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8260" type="x-p"/> The confirmatory clause, <reference osisRef="Job.31.12">Job 31:12</reference>, is co-ordinate with the preceding: for it (this criminal, adulterous enterprise) is a fire, a fire consuming him who allows the sparks of sinful desire to rise up within him (Pro 6:27.; Sir. 9:8), which devours even to the bottom of the abyss, not resting before it has dragged him whom it has seized down with it into the deepest depth of ruin, and as it were melted him away, and which ought to root out all my produce (all the fruit of my labour).<note placement="foot">It is something characteristically Semitic to express the notion of destruction by the figure of burning up with fire [<hi type="italic">vid. supra,</hi> p. 449, note], and it is so much used in the present day as a natural inalienable form of thought, that in curses and imprecations everything, without distinction of the object, is to be burned; e.g., <hi type="italic">juhrik</hi>, may (God) burn up, or <hi type="italic">juhrak</hi>, ought to burn, <hi type="italic">bilâduh</hi>, his native country, <hi type="italic">bedenuh</hi>, his body, <hi type="italic">‛ênuh</hi>, his eye, <hi type="italic">shawâribuh</hi>, his moustache (i.e., his honour), <hi type="italic">nefesuh</hi>, his breath, <hi type="italic">‛omruh</hi>, his life, etc. - Wetzst.</note> <div eID="gen8260" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8261" type="x-p"/> The function of ב is questionable. Ew. (§217, <hi type="italic">f</hi>) explains it as local: in my whole revenue, i.e., throughout my whole domain. But it can also be <hi type="italic">Beth objecti,</hi> whether it be that the obj. is conceived as the means of the action (vid., on <reference osisRef="Job.16.4-Job.16.5">Job 16:4-5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.16.10">Job 16:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.20.20">Job 20:20</reference>), or that, “corresponding to the Greek genitive, it does not express an entire full coincidence, but an action about and upon the object” (Ew. §217, S. 557). We take it as <hi type="italic">Beth obj.</hi> in the latter sense, after the analogy of the so-called pleonastic Arab. <hi type="italic">b</hi> (e.g., <hi type="italic">qaraa bi - suwari ,</hi> he has practised the act of reading upon the Suras of the Koran); and which ought to undertake the act of outrooting upon my whole produce.<note placement="foot">On this pleonastic <hi type="italic">Beth obj.</hi> (<hi type="italic">el - Bâ el - mezı̂de</hi>) vid., Samachschari’s <hi type="italic">Mufassal, ed. Broch,</hi> pp. 125, 132 (according to which it serves “to give intensity and speciality”), and Beidhâwi’s observation on <hi type="italic">Sur</hi>. ii. 191. The most usual example for it is <hi type="italic">alqa bi - jedeihi ila et - tahlike ,</hi> he has plunged his hands, i.e., himself, into ruin. The <hi type="italic">Bâ el - megâ z</hi> (the metaphorical <hi type="italic">Beth obj.</hi>) is similar; it is used where the verb has not its most natural signification but a metaphorical one, e.g., <hi type="italic">ashada bidhikrihi ,</hi> he has strengthened his memory: comp. De Sacy, <hi type="italic">Chrestomathie Arabe,</hi> i. 397.</note>
entries.c5ffb289d2041079c39196a0bb4940f78478e2f4: <reference osisRef="Job.31.13-Job.15.13">Job 31:13-15 13</reference>  If I despised the cause of my servant and my maid, <div eID="gen8261" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8262" type="x-p"/> When they contended with me: 14  What should I do, if God should rise up, <div eID="gen8262" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8263" type="x-p"/> And if He should make search, what should I answer Him? 15  Hath not He who formed me in the womb formed him also, <div eID="gen8263" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8264" type="x-p"/> And hath not One fashioned us in the belly? <div eID="gen8264" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8265" type="x-p"/> It might happen, as <reference osisRef="Job.31.13">Job 31:13</reference> assumes, that his servant or his maid (אמה, Arab. <hi type="italic">amatun ,</hi> denotes a maid who is not necessarily a slave, <hi type="italic">‛abde</hi>, as <reference osisRef="Job.19.15">Job 19:15</reference>, whereas שׁפחה does not occur in the book) contended with him, and in fact so that they on their part began the dispute (for, as the Talmud correctly points out, it is not בּריבי עמּם, but בּריבם עמּדי), but he did not then treat them as a despot; they were not accounted as <hi type="italic">res</hi> but <hi type="italic">personae</hi> by him, he allowed them to maintain their personal right in opposition to him. Christopher Scultetus observes here: <hi type="italic">Gentiles quidem non concedebant jus servo contra dominum, cui etiam vitae necisque potestas in ipsum erat; sed Iob amore justitiae libere se demisit, ut vel per alios judices aut arbitros litem talem curaret decidi vel sibi ipsi sit moderatus, ut juste pronuntiaret.</hi> If he were one who despised (אמאס not מאסתּי) his servants’ cause: what should he do if God arose and entered into judgment; and if He should appoint an examination (thus Hahn correctly, for the conclusion shows that פקד is here a synon. of בחן <reference osisRef="Ps.17.3">Psa 17:3</reference>, and חקר <reference osisRef="Ps.44.22">Psa 44:22</reference>, Arab. <hi type="italic">fqd</hi>, V, VIII, <hi type="italic">accurate inspicere</hi>), what should he answer?
entries.d79d4387dd0f0e058cd8dabdc95f89a6cec33cf2: <reference osisRef="Job.31.16-Job.18.16">Job 31:16-18 16</reference>  If I held back the poor from what they desired, <div eID="gen8266" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8267" type="x-p"/> And caused the eyes of the widow to languish, 17  And ate my morsel alone <div eID="gen8267" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8268" type="x-p"/> Without letting the fatherless eat thereof: - 18  No indeed, from my youth he grew up to me as to a father, <div eID="gen8268" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8269" type="x-p"/> And from my mother’s womb I guided her - <div eID="gen8269" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8270" type="x-p"/> The whole strophe is the hypothetical antecedent of the imprecative conclusion, <reference osisRef="Job.31.22">Job 31:22</reference>, which closes the following strophe. Since מנע דּבר ממּנוּ, <hi type="italic">cohibere aliquid ab aliquo</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.22.7">Job 22:7</reference>), is said as much in accordance with the usage of the language as מנעו מדּבר, <hi type="italic">cohibere aliquem ab aliquo</hi> (Num 24:11; <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.10">Ecc 2:10</reference>), in the sense of <hi type="italic">denegare alicui aliquid</hi>, there is no reason for taking מחפץ דּלּים together as a genitival clause (<hi type="italic">a voto tenuium</hi>), as the accentuation requires it. On חפץ, vid., on <reference osisRef="Job.21.21">Job 21:21</reference>; it signifies solicitude (what is ardently desired) and business, here the former: what is ever the interest and want of the poor (the reduced or those without means). From such like things he does not keep the poor back, i.e., does not refuse them; and the eyes of the widow he did not cause or allow to languish (כּלּה, to bring to an end, i.e., cause to languish, of the eyes, as <reference osisRef="Lev.26.16">Lev 26:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.33">1Sa 2:33</reference>); he let not their longing for assistance be consumed of itself, let not the fountain of their tears become dry without effect. If he had done the opposite, if he had eaten his bread (פּת = פּת לחם) alone, and not allowed the orphan to eat of it with him - but no, he had not acted thus; on the contrary (כּי as <reference osisRef="Ps.130.4">Psa 130:4</reference> and frequently), he (the parentless one) grew up to him (גּדלני = גּדל לּי, Ges. §121, 4, according to Ew. §315, <hi type="italic">b</hi>, “by the interweaving of the dialects of the people into the ancient form of the declining language;” perhaps it is more correct to say it is by virtue of a poetic, forced, and rare brevity of expression) as to a father (= לאב כּמו), and from his mother’s womb he guided her, the helpless and defenceless widow, like a faithful child leading its sick or aged mother. The hyperbolical expression מבּטן אמּי dates this sympathizing and active charity back to the very beginning of Job’s life. He means to say that it is in-born to him, and he has exercised it ever since he was first able to do so. The brevity of the form גּדלני, brief to incorrectness, might be removed by the pointing גּדּלני (Olsh.): from my youth up he (the fatherless one) honoured me as a father; and גּדּלני (instead of כּבּדני would be explained by the consideration, that a veneration is meant that attributed a dignity which exceed his age to the נער who was not yet old enough to be a father. But גּדּל signifies “to cause to grow” in such a connection elsewhere (parall. רומם, to raise), wherefore lxx translates ἐξέτρεφον (גּדּלתּי); and גּדלני has similar examples of the construction of intransitives with the <hi type="italic">acc</hi>. instead of the <hi type="italic">dat</hi>. (especially Zec 7:5) in its favour: they became me great, i.e., became great in respect of me. Other ways of getting over the difficulty are hardly worth mentioning: the Syriac version reads כּאב (pain) and אנחות; Raschi makes <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.31.18">Job 31:18</reference></hi>, the idea of benevolence, the subj., and <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.31.18">Job 31:18</reference></hi> (as מדּה, attribute) the obj. The <hi type="italic">suff</hi>. of אנחנּה Schlottm. refers to the female orphan; but Job refers again to the orphan in the following strophe, and the reference to the widow, more natural here on account of the gender, has nothing against it. The choice of the verb (comp. <reference osisRef="Job.38.32">Job 38:32</reference>) also corresponds to such a reference, since the <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. has an intensified <hi type="italic">Kal</hi>-signification here.<note placement="foot">זכר and הזכיר, to remember; זרע and הזריע, to sow, to cover with seed; חרשׁ and החרישׁ, both in the signification <hi type="italic">silere</hi> and <hi type="italic">fabricari;</hi> לעג and הלעיג, to mock, <reference osisRef="Job.21.3">Job 21:3</reference>; משׁל and המשׁיל, <hi type="italic">dominari</hi>, <reference osisRef="Job.25.2">Job 25:2</reference>; נטה and הטה, to extend, to bow; קנה ;w and הקנה (to obtain by purchase); קצר and הקציר, to reap, <reference osisRef="Job.24.6">Job 24:6</reference>, are all similar. In Arab. the <hi type="italic">Kal nahaituhu</hi> signifies I put him aside by going on one side (<hi type="italic">nahw</hi> or <hi type="italic">nâhije</hi>), the <hi type="italic">Hiph. anhaituhu ,</hi> I put him aside by bringing him to the side (comp. ינחם, <reference osisRef="Job.12.23">Job 12:23</reference>).</note> <div eID="gen8270" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8271" type="x-p"/> From earliest youth, so far back as he can remember, he was wont to behave like a father to the orphan, and like a child to the widow.
entries.a88183f784823dcb04a31faef86c650734b530fd: Job 31:19-23 19  If I saw one perishing without clothing, <div eID="gen8271" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8272" type="x-p"/> And that the needy had no covering; 20  If his loins blessed me not, <div eID="gen8272" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8273" type="x-p"/> And he did not warm himself from the hide of my lambs; 21  If I have lifted up my hand over the orphan, <div eID="gen8273" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8274" type="x-p"/> Because I saw my help in the gate: 22  Let my shoulder fall out of its shoulder-blade, <div eID="gen8274" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8275" type="x-p"/> And mine arm be broken from its bone; 23  For terror would come upon me, the destruction of God, <div eID="gen8275" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8276" type="x-p"/> And before His majesty I should not be able to stand. <div eID="gen8276" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8277" type="x-p"/> On אובד comp. on <reference osisRef="Job.4.11">Job 4:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.29.13">Job 29:13</reference>; he who is come down from his right place and is perishing (root בד, to separate, still perfectly visible through the Arab. <hi type="italic">bâda , ba‛ida ,</hi> to perish), or also he who is already perished, <hi type="italic">periens</hi> and <hi type="italic">perditus</hi>. The clause, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.31.19">Job 31:19</reference></hi>, forms the second obj. to אם אראה, which otherwise signifies <hi type="italic">si video,</hi> but here, in accordance with the connection, signifies <hi type="italic">si videbam.</hi> The blessing of the thankful (<reference osisRef="Job.29.13">Job 29:13</reference>) is transferred from the person to the limbs in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.31.20">Job 31:20</reference></hi>, which need and are benefited by the warmth imparted. אם־לא here is not an expression of an affirmative asseveration, but a negative turn to the continuation of the hypothetical antecedents. The shaking, הניף, of the hand, <reference osisRef="Job.31.21">Job 31:21</reference>, is intended, like <reference osisRef="Isa.11.15">Isa 11:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.19.16">Isa 19:16</reference> (comp. the <hi type="italic">Pilel</hi>, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.32">Isa 10:32</reference>), Zec 2:13, as a preparation for a crushing stroke. Job refrained himself from such designs upon the defenceless orphan, even when he saw his help in the gate, i.e., before the tribunal (<reference osisRef="Job.29.7">Job 29:7</reference>), i.e., even when he had a certain prospect or powerful assistance there. If he has acted otherwise, his כּתף, i.e., his upper arm together with the shoulder, must fall out from its שׁכם, i.e., the back which bears it together with the shoulder-blades, and his אזרע, upper and lower arm, which is considered here according to its outward flesh, must be broken out of its קנה, tube, i.e., the reed-like hollow bone which gives support to it, i.e., be broken asunder from its basis (Syr. <hi type="italic">a radice sua</hi>), this sinning arm, which did not compassionate the naked, and mercilessly threatened the defenceless and helpless. The ת <hi type="italic">raphatum</hi> which follows in both cases, and the express testimony of the Masora, show that משּׁכמה and מקּנה have no <hi type="italic">Mappik</hi>. The <hi type="italic">He quiescens,</hi> however, is in both instances softened from the <hi type="italic">He mappic.</hi> of the <hi type="italic">suff.,</hi> Ew. §21,f. פּחד in <reference osisRef="Job.31.23">Job 31:23</reference> is taken by most expositors as predicate: for terror is (was) to me evil as God, the righteous judge, decrees it. But אלי is not favourable to this. It establishes the particular thing which he imprecates upon himself, and that consequently which, according to his own conviction and perception, ought justly to overtake him out of the general mass, viz., that terror ought to come upon him, a divine decreed weight of affliction. איד אל is a permutative of פחד = פחד אלהים, and אלי with <hi type="italic">Dechî</hi> equivalent to אלי (יבא) יהיה, comp. <reference osisRef="Jer.2.19">Jer 2:19</reference> (where it is to be interpreted: and that thou lettest no fear before me come over thee). Thus also <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.31.23">Job 31:23</reference></hi> is suitably connected with the preceding: and I should not overcome His majesty, i.e., I should succumb to it. The מן corresponds to the <hi type="italic">prae</hi> in <hi type="italic">praevalerem;</hi> שׂאת (lxx falsely, λῆμμα, judgment, decision = משׂא, Jer. <hi type="italic">pondus</hi>) is not intended otherwise than <reference osisRef="Job.13.11">Job 13:11</reference> (parall. פחד as here).
entries.b8037a3f3c4e4de1b27180e3702bc4c5682303ba: <reference osisRef="Job.31.24-Job.28.24">Job 31:24-28 24</reference>  If I made gold my confidence, <div eID="gen8277" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8278" type="x-p"/> And said to the fine gold: O my trust; 25  If I rejoiced that my wealth was great, <div eID="gen8278" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8279" type="x-p"/> And that my hand had gained much; - 26  If I saw the sunlight when it shone, <div eID="gen8279" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8280" type="x-p"/> And the moon walking in splendour, 27  And my heart was secretly enticed, <div eID="gen8280" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8281" type="x-p"/> And I threw them a kiss by my hand: 28  This also would be a punishable crime, <div eID="gen8281" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8282" type="x-p"/> For I should have played the hypocrite to God above. <div eID="gen8282" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8283" type="x-p"/> Not only from covetous extortion of another’s goods was he conscious of being clear, but also from an excessive delight in earthly possessions. He has not made gold his כּסל, confidence (vid., on כּסלתך, <reference osisRef="Job.4.6">Job 4:6</reference>); he has not said to כּתם, fine gold (pure, <reference osisRef="Job.28.19">Job 28:19</reference>, of Ophir, <reference osisRef="Job.28.16">Job 28:16</reference>), מבטחי (with <hi type="italic">Dag. forte implicitum</hi> as <reference osisRef="Job.8.14">Job 8:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.18.14">Job 18:14</reference>): object (ground) of my trust! He has not rejoiced that his wealth is great (רב, adj.), and that his hand has attained כּבּיר, something great (neutral <hi type="italic">masc</hi>. Ew. §172, <hi type="italic">b</hi>).
